, in order to check that we indeed get a
4
-cut. This procedure is shown in Algorithm
22
. The proof of correctness and linear complexity is given in Proposition
11.4
.

Lemma 11.3
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
M(v)
has a child
c
. Let
u
be a proper descendant of
u
such that
M(u)
is a descendant of
c
, and let
w
be a proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
. Then there is a back-edge
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
such that
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
if and only if:
\mathit{high}(u)<v
,
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
.

Proof.

(
\Rightarrow
)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
is an immediate consequence of
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
. Since
B(u)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(v)\setminus\{e\}
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)
, we have that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}(u)<v
(because every back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)
must have
y<v
). Since
B(u)\cap B(w)\neq\emptyset
and
w
is a proper ancestor of
u
, we have that the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
is in
B(w)
. And since
(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=\emptyset
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(w)
, we have that the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
is precisely
e
. Then, since
(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=\emptyset
and
u
is a proper descendant of
w
, we have that no back-edge
e^{\prime}
in
B(u)\setminus\{e\}
has lower point that is lower than
w
(because this would imply that
e^{\prime}\in B(w)
). This implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
.

(
\Leftarrow
)
Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore a descendant of
c
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
(x,y)
is a back-edge,
y
is an ancestor of
x
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
y
, and therefore
v
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)
, and therefore
y\leq\mathit{high}(u)
. Thus,
\mathit{high}(u)<v
implies that
y<v
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that

. Since

, by Lemma

.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that

. Then,

and
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
imply that

, and therefore
\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)\leq\mathit{bcount}(v)
, in contradiction to
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Thus, we have that

.

Let

be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that

. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e\notin B(w)
. Consider a back-edge
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u)\setminus\{(x,y)\}
. Then, we have that

. Thus,
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
implies that
y^{\prime}\geq w
. This implies that
y^{\prime}
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore

. Due to the generality of

, this implies that

. Therefore, since

, we have that
B(w)\cap B(u)=\emptyset
, a contradiction. Thus, we have that

. Furthermore, since
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
, this is the only back-edge in
B(u)
that is also in
B(w)
.

Thus, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(u)\cap B(w)=\{e\}
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)=((B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\}))\sqcup\{e\}
, and therefore
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.
∎

.

Proof.

11.1.2

of Lemma

M(u^{\prime})=M(u)
and
u^{\prime}<u
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(u^{\prime})\subset B(u)
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u)\setminus B(u^{\prime})
. Then,
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v)
, and therefore
y^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u^{\prime})
, a contradiction. Thus, we have that
u
is the lowest proper descendant of
v
such that
M(u)=M(v,c_{2})
.
∎

Lemma 11.6
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(w)
such that
e\notin B(v)\cup B(u)
,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, and
M(v)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Let
c_{1}
be the
\mathit{low1}
child of
M(v)
, and let
w^{\prime}
be the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
with the property that there is a back-edge
e^{\prime}\in B(w^{\prime})
such that
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})=M(v,c_{1})
. Then, we have that
e^{\prime}\notin B(v)\cup B(u)
,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
and
M(v)\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Furthermore, if
w^{\prime}\neq w
, then
B(w)\sqcup\{e^{\prime}\}=B(w^{\prime})\sqcup\{e\}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
11.5
we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
,
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(w)
, and
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v,c_{1})
. Thus, we may consider the greatest ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
\mathit{low}(u)
with the property that there is a back-edge
e^{\prime}\in B(w^{\prime})
such that
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})=M(v,c_{1})
. We may assume that
w^{\prime}\neq w
, because otherwise there is nothing to show. Thus we have
w^{\prime}>w
. Notice that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
, and therefore the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
is in
B(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u)
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore
w^{\prime}
is also a proper ancestor of
v
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that the higher endpoint of
e^{\prime}
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
. If
(x,y)=e^{\prime}
, then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Otherwise, if
(x,y)\neq e^{\prime}
, then we have that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Thus, in any case we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
, this implies that
M(w^{\prime})
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. But we have
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
, and therefore
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
, and therefore
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})=M(w^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that the higher endpoint of
e^{\prime}
is not a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
. Similarly, we can see that the higher endpoint of
e
is not a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.

Since
v
is a common descendant of
w
and
w^{\prime}
, we have that
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}>w
implies that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v,c_{1})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Since
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
, we have that
x
is not the higher endpoint of
e^{\prime}
, and therefore
(x,y)\neq e^{\prime}
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
can be strengthened to
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, this implies that
B(w)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v,c_{1})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. The case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected, because
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
(and therefore there is no back-edge in
B(u)
whose lower endpoint is low enough to be a proper ancestor of
w
). Thus, we have
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}
, this implies that
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}\subseteq B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Thus, since we have showed the reverse inclusion too, we have that
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Then,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e\in B(w^{\prime})
. Then, since
e\in B(w)
and
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, we have that
e=e^{\prime}
and
B(w^{\prime})=B(w)
, which contradicts the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus,
e\notin B(w^{\prime})
. Similarly, we have
e^{\prime}\notin B(w)
. Thus,
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
implies that
B(w^{\prime})\sqcup\{e\}=B(w)\sqcup\{e^{\prime}\}
. Since
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
, we have
B(u)\cap B(w^{\prime})=\emptyset
. In particular, this implies that
e^{\prime}\notin B(u)
. Therefore,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
implies that
e^{\prime}\notin B(u)\cup B(v)
.
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})=M(v,c_{1})
implies that
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
is a descendant of
c_{1}
, and therefore a proper descendant of
M(v)
. Thus,
M(v)\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e^{\prime}\})
.
∎

Now we have collected enough information in order to show how to compute a collection of Type-3
\beta i

4
-cuts that satisfy
(2)
of Lemma
11.1
, so that all
4
-cuts of this type are implied by this collection, plus that returned by Algorithm

. Based on Lemma

, it is sufficient to compute all Type-3
\beta i

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
, such that

satisfies
(2)
of Lemma

, where

is the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v,c_{1})
, where
c_{1}
is the
\mathit{low1}
child of
M(v)
. By Lemma

we have that either

, or

. Thus, we distinguish two cases, depending on whether

or

. By Lemma

, we have that
u
is the lowest proper descendant of

, where

Lemma 11.7
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
M(v)
has at least two distinct children
c_{1}
and
c_{2}
. Let
w
be a proper ancestor of
v
with the property that
M(w)\neq M(v)
and there is a back-edge
e
such that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
is a descendant of
c_{1}
, and let
u
be a proper descendant of
v
such that
M(u)
is a descendant of
c_{2}
. Suppose that
\mathit{high}(u)<v
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Then,
e\notin B(u)\cup B(v)
and
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.

Proof.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
y
, and therefore
v
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)
, and therefore
y\leq\mathit{high}(u)
. Thus,
\mathit{high}(u)<v
implies that
y<v
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore a descendant of
c_{1}
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, this implies that
B(w)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Then
x
is a descendant of both
M(u)
and
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore a descendant of both
c_{2}
and
c_{1}
. This implies that
c_{1}
and
c_{2}
are related as ancestor and descendant, which is absurd. Thus, we have that
B(u)\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=\emptyset
.

Then, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
and
B(w)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(v)
and
B(u)\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=\emptyset
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e\in B(u)
. Let
x
be the higher endpoint of
e
. Notice that
M(w)=\mathit{nca}\{x,M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})\}
. Since
e\in B(u)
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore a descendant of
c_{2}
. Since
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v,c_{1})
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
is a descendant of
c_{1}
. Thus, we have that
\mathit{nca}\{x,M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})\}=M(v)
, in contradiction to the assumption
M(w)\neq M(v)
. This shows that
e\notin B(u)
. Thus,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
e\notin B(u)\cup B(v)
.
∎

. Then we have that

\beta i

w\in W_{L}(M(v,c_{1}))
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v,c_{1})
. This implies that
M(v,c_{1})
is a common descendant of
v
and
w
, and therefore
v
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant. Notice that, since we have reached Line
23
, we have that
u
in Line
23
satisfies
M(u)=M(v,c_{2})
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u)<v
. To see this, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
x
is a descendant of
c_{2}
. (Such a back-edge exists, because
\mathit{low}(c_{2})<v
, since we have passed the check in Line
23
.) Then
x
is a descendant of
M(v,c_{2})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(u)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Therefore, since
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
and
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, we have
\mathit{low}(u)<v
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)
is an ancestor of
y
, and therefore an ancestor of
v
. Then, since
v
is a common descendant of
\mathit{low}(u)
and
w
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant, and then
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus,
w
is the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{low}(u)
such that
w\in W_{L}(M(v,c_{1}))
. Now, since the total number of all
q^{\prime}
queries is
O(n)
, and since the sets
W_{L}
are pairwise disjoint, by Lemma
8.5
we have that Algorithm
12
can answer all those queries in linear time in total.
We conclude that Algorithm
23
runs in linear time.
∎

11.1.3

of Lemma

Lemma 11.9

We distinguish two cases for the Type-3
\beta i

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
, where
u
is a descendant of
v
,
v
is a descendant of
w
, and

satisfies
(3)
of Lemma

: either
M(u)=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, or
M(u)\neq M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. In the first case, we can compute all such
4
-cuts explicitly. In the second case, we compute only a subcollection
\mathcal{C}
of them, so that the rest are implied by
\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
, where
\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
is the collection of Type-
2ii

4
-cuts that are computed by Algorithm
14
. Our result is summarized and proved in Proposition
11.13
.

The reason that the
4
-cuts in the first case can be computed explicitly is the following.

Lemma 11.10
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
v
is a proper descendant of
w
, and
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
, where
e
is a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
e\notin B(v)
. Suppose that
M(u)=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. Then
u
is either the lowest or the second-lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
.

Proof.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is neither the lowest nor the second-lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
. This means that there are two proper descendants
u^{\prime}
and
u^{\prime\prime}
of
v
, such that
u>u^{\prime}>u^{\prime\prime}
and
M(u^{\prime})=M(u^{\prime\prime})=M(u)
. Since
M(u)=M(u^{\prime})=M(u^{\prime\prime})
, we have that
u
,
u^{\prime}
and
u^{\prime\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant, and therefore
u>u^{\prime}>u^{\prime\prime}
implies that
u
is a proper descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
u^{\prime\prime}
. Then, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(u^{\prime\prime})\subseteq B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(u^{\prime\prime})\subset B(u^{\prime})\subset B(u)
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus B(u^{\prime})
, and a back-edge
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus B(u^{\prime\prime})
. Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Thus, since
(x,y)\notin B(u^{\prime})
, we have that
y
is not a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This implies that
y
is not a proper ancestor of
v
either, and therefore
(x,y)\notin B(v)
. Similarly, since
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus B(u^{\prime\prime})
, we have that
y^{\prime}
is not a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime\prime}
, and therefore not a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\notin B(v)
. Notice that both
(x,y)
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
are in
B(u)
(since
B(u^{\prime\prime})\subset B(u^{\prime})\subset B(u)
). Furthermore, since
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u^{\prime})
and
(x,y)\notin B(u^{\prime})
, we have that
(x,y)\neq(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
. Thus,
(x,y)
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
are two distinct back-edges in
B(u)
that are not in
B(v)
. But this contradicts the fact
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
, which implies that
e
is the only back-edge from
B(u)
that is not in
B(v)
. This shows that
u
is either the lowest or the second-lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
.
∎

In the case where
M(u)\neq M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, we consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v
that satisfies
M(u^{\prime})\neq M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. Then, the following shows that we still get a Type-
3\beta i

4
-cut with
v
and
w
.

Lemma 11.11
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(u)
such that
e\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
and
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
. Suppose that
M(u)\neq M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. Let
u^{\prime}
be the lowest proper descendant of
v
such that
M(u^{\prime})\neq M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. Then we have
e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
and
B(v)=(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})\sqcup B(w)
. Furthermore, if
u^{\prime}\neq u
, then
B(u)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}=B(u^{\prime})\sqcup\{e\}
.

Proof.

By the proof of Lemma
11.9
, we have
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(u)
. (This result does not rely on the supposition
M(w)\neq M(v)
, which is included in the statement of Lemma
11.9
.) Thus, it makes sense to consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v
that satisfies
M(u^{\prime})\neq M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
. If
u^{\prime}=u
, then there is nothing to show. So let us assume that
u^{\prime}\neq u
. Then, due to the minimality of
u^{\prime}
, we have
u^{\prime}<u
. Since
M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, we have that
M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
is a common descendant of
u
and
u^{\prime}
. Therefore,
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant, and then
u^{\prime}<u
implies that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
.

Since
M(u^{\prime})\neq M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})
is the only back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})
. Similarly, since
M(u)\neq M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, we have that
e
is the only back-edge in
B(u)
whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(u)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
, this implies that

. Since the higher endpoint of

is not a descendant of

, we have that

. Thus,
B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(u)
can be strengthened to

. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)\setminus\{e\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(u^{\prime})
. Furthermore,

implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e\}
, this implies that
B(u)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. Since the higher endpoint of
e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
M(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})=M(B(u)\setminus\{e\})
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\notin B(u)\setminus\{e\}
. Thus,
B(u)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
can be strengthened to
B(u)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
.

Thus, we have shown that
B(u)\setminus\{e\}=B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
. Then, notice that we cannot have
e\in B(u^{\prime})
or
e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\in B(u)
, because otherwise we get
B(u)=B(u^{\prime})
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus,

implies that
B(u)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}=B(u^{\prime})\sqcup\{e\}
. Furthermore, since
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
and
B(u)\setminus\{e\}=B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
, we infer that
B(v)=(B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\})\sqcup B(w)
.

Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have
|(B(u^{\prime})|>1
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u^{\prime})\}
. Then we have that

is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Thus, since

, we have that

. Since

is a back-edge,

and

and

. Since

Lemma 11.12
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
M(v)
has at least two children. Let
u
be a proper descendant of
v
such that
M(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
, and let
w
be a proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. Suppose that
M(u)
and
M(w)
are not related as ancestor and descendant,
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)<v
, and
\mathit{bcount}(u)=\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
. Then,
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
and
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
.

Proof.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge,
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
y
and
v
, and therefore
y
and
v
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)
, and therefore
y\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)<v
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
, this implies that
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}\subseteq B(v)
.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)
, this implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
B(u)\cap B(w)\neq\emptyset
. Then there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\cap B(w)
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of both
M(u)
and
M(w)
, and therefore
M(u)
and
M(w)
are related as ancestor and descendant. A contradiction. Thus, we have that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
.

Now, since
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}\subseteq B(v)
,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
and
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, we have that
(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)\subseteq B(v)
. Then,
\mathit{bcount}(u)=\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
implies that
(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)=B(v)
. Since
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(w)
. Thus,
(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)=B(v)
implies that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(v)
, and so we have
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
.
∎

Lemma 11.15
.

Lemma 11.16
.

Let

be three vertices
\neq r
such that

Lemma 11.17
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(v)
such that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(w)
. Suppose that
M(v)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
. Then
u
is the lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
. In case
(w.1)
of Lemma
11.16
we have that
w
is either the greatest or the second-greatest proper ancestor of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(w))
. In case
(w.2)
of Lemma
11.16
we have that
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(w))
.

Proof.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not the lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
. This means that there is a proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v
such that
u^{\prime}<u
and
M(u^{\prime})=M(u)
. This implies that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and then Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(u^{\prime})\subset B(u)
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus B(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(u)=M(u^{\prime})
. Furthermore,
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. But this shows that
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, a contradiction. Thus,
u
is the lowest proper descendant of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(u))
.

Let
c_{1}
,
c_{2}
and
c_{3}
be the
\mathit{low1}
,
\mathit{low2}
and
\mathit{low3}
children of
M(v)
, respectively. Then Lemma
11.16
implies that
M(u)
is either a descendant of
c_{2}
or a descendant of
c_{3}
. In either case, then, we have that no descendant of
M(u)
can be a descendant of
c_{1}
. Furthermore, Lemma
11.16
implies that either
(w.1)

M(w)=M(v,c_{1})
, or
(w.2)

M(w)=M(v,c_{1}^{\prime})
, where
c_{1}^{\prime}
is the
\mathit{low1}
child of
M(v,c_{1})
.

Let us assume first that
(w.1)
is true. That is, we have
M(w)=M(v,c_{1})
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w
is neither the greatest nor the second-greatest proper ancestor of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(w))
. This means that there are proper ancestors
w^{\prime}
and
w^{\prime\prime}
of
v
such that
w^{\prime\prime}>w^{\prime}>w
and
M(w^{\prime\prime})=M(w^{\prime})=M(w)
. This implies that
w^{\prime\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w^{\prime}
, and
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
. Then, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(w^{\prime})\subseteq B(w^{\prime\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime})\subset B(w^{\prime\prime})
. Thus, there are back-edges
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(w^{\prime\prime})\setminus B(w^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})=M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v,c_{1})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. The case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected, because it implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore it is not a descendant of
c_{1}
, whereas
x
is a descendant of

, and therefore a descendant of
c_{1}
. The case
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected because
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
. Thus, the only viable option is
(x,y)=e
. Then, with the same argument we can show that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=e
, and therefore we have
(x,y)=(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
. But this contradicts the fact that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\notin B(w^{\prime})
. Thus, we have shown that
w
is either the greatest or the second-greatest proper ancestor of
v
in
M^{-1}(M(w))
.

Now let us assume that
(w.2)
is true. That is, we have
M(w)=M(v,c_{1}^{\prime})
, where

is the
\mathit{low1}
child of

. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that the higher endpoint of
e
is a descendant of
c_{1}^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
x
is a descendant of
c_{1}
. Then

implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. The case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected, because it implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore it is not a descendant of
c_{1}
, whereas we have that
x
is a descendant of
c_{1}
. Thus, we have that either
(x,y)\in B(w)
or
(x,y)=e
. If
(x,y)\in B(w)
, then
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v,c_{1}^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
c_{1}^{\prime}
. If
(x,y)=e
, then by supposition we have that
x
is a descendant of
c_{1}^{\prime}
. In either case, then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
c_{1}^{\prime}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
such that

is a descendant of
c_{1}
, this implies that
M(v,c_{1})
is a descendant of
c_{1}^{\prime}
. But this is impossible, because

is a child of

. Thus, we have that the higher endpoint of

is not a descendant of

.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that

is not the greatest proper ancestor of

in

. This means that there is a proper ancestor

of

such that

. This implies that

, and therefore Lemma

. Since the graph is

. Thus, there is a back-edge

. Then

. Furthermore,

, and therefore a proper ancestor of

. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then

implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or

, or
(x,y)=e
. The case

is rejected, because it implies that

is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore it is not a descendant of

, whereas

is a descendant of

, and therefore a descendant of

. The case

. Thus, we conclude that

in

.

Lemma 11.18
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
, and
v
is a proper descendant of
w
. Suppose that
(1)

M(u)
and
M(w)
are descendants of
M(v)
that are not related as ancestor and descendant,
(2)

\mathit{high}(u)<v
, and
(3)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
. Then there is a back-edge
e
such that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
.

Proof.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(u)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)
, and therefore
y\leq\mathit{high}(u)
. Then,
\mathit{high}(u)<v
implies that
y<v
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
y
, and therefore
v
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then,
y<v
implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
.
Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)
, this implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
.
Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
B(u)\cap B(w)\neq\emptyset
. Then there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\cap B(w)
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of both
M(u)
and
M(w)
, contradicting the fact that
M(u)
and
M(w)
are not related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, we have
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
.
Now, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, we infer that there is a back-edge
e
such that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
.
∎

B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
. Then Lemma
11.14
implies that
e=e(u,v,w)
. Thus,
C
is a
4
-cut that satisfies
(4)
of Lemma
11.1
, and therefore it is correctly marked as a
4
-cut.

Now we will argue about the complexity of Algorithm
26
. For every vertex
v\neq r
, we generate queries for computing
M(v,c_{1}(v))
,
M(v,c_{2}(v))
and
M(v,c_{3}(v))
(for those of
c_{1}(v)
,
c_{2}(v)
and
c_{3}(v)
that exist). By Proposition
6.18
, we can have the answer to all those queries in linear time in total. Then, for every
v\neq r
such that
M(v,c_{1}(v))\neq\bot
and
c_{1}^{\prime}(v)\neq\bot
, we generate a query for computing
M(v,c_{1}^{\prime}(v))
. Similarly, if
M(v,c_{2}(v))\neq\bot
, then we generate queries for computing
M(v,c_{1}^{\prime\prime}(v))
and
M(v,c_{2}^{\prime\prime}(v))
(for those of
c_{1}^{\prime\prime}(v)
and
c_{2}^{\prime\prime}(v)
that exist). According to Proposition
6.18
, all those queries can be answered in linear time in total. We keep pointers from every vertex
v
to all its respective values that were computed (i.e., a pointer to
M(v,c_{1}(v))
, a pointer to
M(v,c_{1}^{\prime\prime}(v))
, etc.). In order to get the vertices
u
and
w
throughout (e.g., in Line
26
and Line
26
), we first collect all the queries for those vertices, and we make appropriate use of Algorithm
12
. The way to do this (and the guarantee of correctness) has been already explained in previous algorithms (e.g., in the proof of Proposition
11.8
). By Lemma
8.5
, we can have the answer to all those queries in linear time in total. It is easy to see that all other operations in Algorithm
26
take
O(n)
time in total. We conclude that Algorithm
26
runs in linear time.
∎

11.2
Type-3
\beta ii

4
-cuts

11.2.1
Type-3
\beta ii
-
1

4
-cuts

Now we consider case
(1)
of Lemma
11.1
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
such that
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. By Lemma
11.1
, we have that
C=\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
is a
4
-cut; we call this a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut.

The following lemma provides some useful information concerning this type of
4
-cuts.

Lemma 11.21
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices such that
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut, and let
e
be the back-edge of the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then
e=(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
. Furthermore,
\mathit{low}(u)<w
,
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
,
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
,
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
and
M(w)=M(v)
. Finally, if
u^{\prime}
is a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, then
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut, we have that
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
. Since
e\in B(w)
, we have that the lower endpoint of
e
is strictly lower than
w
. And since
e\in B(u)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)
is at least as low as the lower endpoint of
e
. This shows that
\mathit{low}(u)<w
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<w
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
w
and
y
, and therefore
w
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
y=\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
and
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<w
, we have
y<w
. This implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. With the same argument, we have that the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
is also in
B(w)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut, we have
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Since
e\in B(u)\cap B(w)
, this implies that there is only one back-edge in
B(u)\cap B(w)
, a contradiction. Thus, we have
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
. Furthermore, since
e\in B(u)\cap B(w)
, we have that
e
is the only back-edge in
B(u)
whose lower endpoint is low enough to be lower than
w
, and therefore
e
is the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
.

Since
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)
, we have
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}(v)\geq\mathit{high}(u)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{high}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
y=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then
y>\mathit{high}(u)
, and therefore
(x,y)\notin B(u)
. Thus,
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Then we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
y<w
. But we have
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)<\mathit{high}(v)=y
, a contradiction. This shows that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
.

Since both
w
and
\mathit{high}(v)
are ancestors of
v
, we have that
w
and
\mathit{high}(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w
is a proper descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{high}(u)
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
y=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. But since
y=\mathit{high}(u)
, this implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<w
, a contradiction. This shows that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
.

Since
B(w)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(v)\setminus\{e\}
and
e\in B(v)\cap B(w)
, we have that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
M(w)
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Since
e\in B(u)
, we have that
M(u)
is an ancestor of the higher endpoint of
e
. Furthermore, since
e\in B(w)
, we have that
M(w)
is an ancestor of the higher endpoint of
e
. Thus, since
M(u)
and
M(w)
have a common descendant, they are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
u
is an ancestor of
M(u)
, this implies that
M(w)
and
u
are also related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradtion, that
M(w)
is not an ancestor of
u
. Then we have that
M(w)
is a proper descendant of
u
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have that there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. But then we have
(x,y)\in(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\cap(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, a contradiction.
Thus, we have that
M(w)
is an ancestor of
u
, and therefore an ancestor of
M(u)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. If
(x,y)=e
, then
e\in B(w)
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
. Otherwise, since
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, we have that either
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e\}
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. If
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e\}
, then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
. If
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, then
M(w)
is an ancestor of
x
. Thus, in every case we have that
M(w)
is an ancestor of
x
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
, this shows that
M(w)
is an ancestor of
M(v)
. Thus, since
M(w)
is a descendant of
M(v)
, we infer that
M(w)=M(v)
.

Now let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
u
is a descendant of
v
and
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is also a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
u\geq u^{\prime}
, we have that either
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
, or it is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u^{\prime}
is not an ancestor of
u
. Then
u^{\prime}
is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
with
y=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Thus,
y=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
implies that
(x,y)
is in
B(v)
. Since
u^{\prime}
is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
, we have that
x
is not a descendant of
u
. Thus,
(x,y)\notin B(u)
. This implies that
e\neq(x,y)
, and thus
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. But
y=\mathit{high}(v)
and
\mathit{high}(v)
is a descendant of
w
, a contradiction. This shows that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.
∎

We will provide a method to compute all Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cuts in linear time. The idea is to compute, for every vertex
v
, a set
U_{1}(v)
of proper descendants
u
of
v
that have the potential to participate in a triple
(u,v,w)
that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut. (These sets have the property that their total size is
O(n)
.) Then, for every
u\in U_{1}(v)
, we search for all
w
with
M(w)=M(v)
that may participate in a triple
(u,v,w)
that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut. (In fact, we can show that such a
w
, if it exists, is unique.) It is sufficient to restrict our search to
w
with
M(w)=M(v)
, according to Lemma
11.21
.

Now let
v\neq r
be a vertex with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. Let
S
be the segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant (i.e., we have
S=S(v)
). Then we let
U_{1}(v)
denote the collection of all vertices
u\in S
such that either
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{nextM}(v)>\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, or
(2)

u
is the lowest proper descendant of
v
in
S
such that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

Lemma 11.22
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta ii
-
1

4
-cut. Then
u\in U_{1}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta ii
-
1

4
-cut, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
, and by Lemma
11.21
we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then Lemma
11.21
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. This shows that
u
and
v
belong to a segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
with the property that its elements are related as ancestors and descendants. Thus, we have
u\in S(v)
.

By Lemma
11.21
we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
. Thus,
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
w\leq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.
Now, if
u
satisfies
\mathit{nextM}(v)>\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, then
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{1}(v)
. Otherwise, if
\mathit{nextM}(v)>\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
is not true, then either
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
or
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Since
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq w
, the case
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<\mathit{lastM}(v)
is rejected by Lemma
11.21
(because this ensures that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
, and we have that
w\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
). Thus we have
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u^{\prime}\in S(v)
that is a proper descendant of
v
, it is lower than
u
, and satisfies
\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.
This implies that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
(because all vertices in
S(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant). Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
, and therefore it is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, and therefore we have
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. This can be strengthened to
B(u)\subset B(u^{\prime})
, since the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus B(u)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
, and therefore it is a proper ancestor of
v
(since
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
). This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
.
Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut, we have
B(v)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(u)\cup B(w)
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
, where
e
is the back-edge of the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Since
(x,y)\in B(v)
and
(x,y)\notin B(u)
, this implies that
(x,y)\neq e
and
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Thus, since
\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we have that
(x,y)=(\mathit{lowD}_{1}(u^{\prime}),\mathit{low}_{1}(u^{\prime}))
, and
(x,y)
is the only back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
whose lower endpoint is lower than
w
. Now, since
e\in B(u)
, we have that the higher endpoint of
e
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Then, since
e\in B(w)
, we have that the lower endpoint of
e
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
e\in B(u^{\prime})
. But we have that
(x,y)
is the only back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
whose lower endpoint is lower than
w
, and therefore
(x,y)=e
, a contradiction. We conclude that
u
is the lowest vertex in
S(v)
that is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
. Thus,
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{1}(v)
.
∎

Lemma 11.23
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
. Suppose that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
and
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
, by Lemma
6.3
we have that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(v^{\prime})\subset B(v)
. This implies that
M(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, Lemma
6.7
implies that
M(v^{\prime})\neq M(v)
(for otherwise we would have
B(v^{\prime})=B(v)
). Thus,
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
.

Now let
w
be a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
, and let
w^{\prime}
be a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
with
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
. Then
\mathit{nextM}(v)\geq w\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\geq w^{\prime}\geq\mathit{lastM}(v^{\prime})
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w\leq w^{\prime}
. Since
w
is an ancestor of
v
, it is also an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Thus,
w
and
w^{\prime}
have
v^{\prime}
as a common descendant, and therefore they are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
w\leq w^{\prime}
, this implies that
w
is an ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}
is a descendant of
v
. This implies that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})=M(w^{\prime})
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
, and thus we have
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
. Conversely, since
M(v^{\prime})=M(w^{\prime})
and
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w^{\prime})\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus we have
B(v^{\prime})=B(w^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that
w^{\prime}
is not a descendant of
v
. Since
w^{\prime}
and
v
have
v^{\prime}
as a common descendant, we have that
w^{\prime}
and
v
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Therefore,
M(v)=M(w)
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Thus, since
w
is an ancestor of
w^{\prime}
and
M(w)
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
, by Lemma
6.1
we have that
M(w)
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
. But
M(w)=M(v)
and
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
, and so we have a contradiction to the fact that
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. This shows that
w>w^{\prime}
. Due to the generality of
w
and
w^{\prime}
, we conclude that
\mathit{lastM}(v)>\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Lemma 11.24
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, such that
S(v^{\prime})=S(v)
and
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
. If
U_{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{1}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{1}(v)
(if it exists) is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{1}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

First, let us suppose that there is a vertex
u
in
U_{1}(v)
. We will show that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. So let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{1}(v)
, we have
u\in S(v)
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}\in S(v^{\prime})=S(v)
, we have that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then, since
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u
and
v^{\prime}
are in
S(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Since
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
and
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
, Lemma
11.23
implies that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Let
w=\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Since
M(w)=M(v^{\prime})
and
w
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus, we have
B(w)\subseteq B(u)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have
|B(w)|\geq 2
. Notice that the lower endpoint of every back-edge in
B(w)
is lower than
w
, and therefore lower than
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Thus,
B(w)\subseteq B(u)
implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, contradicting the fact that
u\in U_{1}(v)
. This shows that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
U_{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
and
U_{1}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be a vertex in
U_{1}(v)
. Then we have shown that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{1}(v)
, we have
u\in S(v)
, and therefore
u\in S(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. By Lemma
11.23
we have
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v^{\prime}
in
S(v^{\prime})
that satisfies
\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. But then we have
u^{\prime}\in U_{1}(v^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that, if
U_{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{1}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{1}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be a vertex in
U_{1}(v)
, and let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex in
U_{1}(v^{\prime})
. We have shown that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{1}(v)
, we have
u\in S(v)=S(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. By Lemma
11.23
we have
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that either
(1)

\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, or
(2)

u^{\prime}
is the lowest vertex in
S(v^{\prime})
that is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
such that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Case
(2)
implies that
u^{\prime}\leq u
(due to the minimality of
u^{\prime}
). So let us assume that case
(1)
is true. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u\leq u^{\prime}
. Since
u\in S(v)
and
u^{\prime}\in S(v^{\prime})
and
S(v)=S(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
u\leq u^{\prime}
implies that
u
is an ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore, we have that
u
and
u^{\prime}
have the same
\mathit{high}
point. Thus, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})
. But we have
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}_{2}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that case
(1)
implies too that
u^{\prime}\leq u
. Due to the generality of
u\in U_{1}(v)
and
u^{\prime}\in U_{1}(v^{\prime})
, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{1}(v)
(if it exists) is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{1}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Based on Lemma
11.24
, we can provide an efficient algorithm for computing the sets
U_{1}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. The computation takes place on segments of
H(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Specifically, let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. Then we have that
U_{1}(v)\subset S(v)
. In other words,
U_{1}(v)
is a subset of the segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. So let
z_{1},\dots,z_{k}
be the vertices of
S(v)
, sorted in decreasing order. Then, we have that
v=z_{i}
, for an
i\in\{1,\dots,k\}
. By definition,
U_{1}(v)
contains every vertex
u
in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
such that either
\mathit{nextM}(v)>\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in this set such that
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

As an implication of Lemma
6.3
, we have that the vertices in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
are sorted in increasing order w.r.t. their
B
set, and therefore they are sorted in decreasing order w.r.t. their
\mathit{low}_{2}
point. In other words, we have
B(z_{1})\subseteq\dots\subseteq B(z_{i-1})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}_{2}(z_{1})\geq\dots\geq\mathit{low}_{2}(z_{i-1})
.
Thus, it is sufficient to process the vertices from
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
in reverse order, in order to find the first vertex
u
that has
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Then, we keep traversing this set in reverse order, and, as long as the
\mathit{low}_{2}
point of every vertex
u
that we meet is lower than
\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we insert
u
into
U_{1}(v)
. Then, once we reach a vertex with
\mathit{low}_{2}
point no lower than
\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we also insert it into
U_{1}(v)
, and we are done.

Now, if there is a proper ancestor
v^{\prime}
of
v
in
S(v)
such that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, then we have that
S(v)=S(v^{\prime})
. If
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, then we have that
U_{1}(v^{\prime})
is defined. Then we can follow the same process as above in order to compute
U_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, according to Lemma
11.24
, it is sufficient to start from the greatest element of
U_{1}(v)
(i.e., the one that was inserted last into
U_{1}(v)
). In particular, if
U_{1}(v)=\emptyset
, then it is certain that
U_{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, and therefore we are done. Otherwise, we just pick up the computation from the greatest vertex in
U_{1}(v)
. In order to perform efficiently those computations, we first compute, for every vertex
x
, the collection
\mathcal{S}(x)
of the segments of
H(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. For every vertex
x
, this computation takes
O(|H(x)|)
time using Algorithm
11
, according to Lemma
6.25
. Since every vertex
\neq r
participates in exactly one set of the form
H(x)
, we have that the total size of all
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for all vertices
x
, is
O(n)
. Then it is sufficient to process separately all segments of
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for every vertex
x
, as described above, by starting the computation each time from the first vertex
v
of the segment that satisfies
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. The whole procedure is shown in Algorithm

. The result is formally stated in Lemma
11.25
.

Lemma 11.25
.

Algorithm

, for all

. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

. It is easy to see that Algorithm

∎

Now we will show how to use the sets
U_{1}
in order to compute all Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cuts.

Corollary 11.26
.

Let
(u,v,w)
and
(u,v,w^{\prime})
be two triples of vertices that induce a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut. Then
w=w^{\prime}
.

Proof.

By Lemma
11.21
we have that the
4
-cuts induced by
(u,v,w)
and
(u,v,w^{\prime})
have the same back-edge (that is,
(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
). Thus, Lemma
3.1
implies that
w=w^{\prime}
.
∎

According to Corollary
11.26
, for every
u\in U_{1}(v)
, where
v\neq r
is a vertex with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
, there is at most one
w
such that
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut. Thus, the idea is to process all
u\in U_{1}(v)
, in order to find the
w
in
M^{-1}(M(v))
(if it exists) such that
(u,v,w)
induces a
4
-cut.

Given a
w
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
w<v
, the following lemma provides a criterion in order to check whether
(u,v,w)
induces a
4
-cut.

Lemma 11.27
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
v
is a proper descendant of
w
,
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
,
M(w)=M(v)
,
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
,
\mathit{low}(u)<w
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Then there is a back-edge
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
such that
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.

Proof.

Since
u
is a descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Since
w
is an ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
. Since
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
, we have that there is at most one back-edge in
B(u)
that may also be in
B(w)
(i.e., the
\mathit{low}
-edge of
u
). Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
w
and
y
, and therefore
w
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then,
y=\mathit{low}(u)<w
implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Therefore, we have that the
\mathit{low}
-edge
e
of
u
is in
B(w)
. Furthermore, since
\mathit{low}(u)<w<v
, the same argument shows that
e\in B(v)
. Now, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(u)\cap B(w)=\{e\}
,
e\in B(v)
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.
∎

Lemma 11.28
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut. Then
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
.

Proof.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a proper ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
v
such that
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
,
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
, and
w^{\prime}>w
. Then we have that
M(w^{\prime})=M(w)
, and so
w^{\prime}
is related as ancestor and descendant with
w
. Since
w^{\prime}>w
, we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
. Thus, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime})
. Similarly, since
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
, we get
B(w^{\prime})\subset B(v)
. Now, since
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime})
, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
. Since
B(w^{\prime})\subset B(v)
, we have that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
, where
e
is the back-edge of the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(v)
implies that either
(1)

(x,y)=e
, or
(2)

(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(3)

(x,y)\in B(w)
. Case
(3)
is immediately rejected, because
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
. Thus,
(1)
is also rejected (since
e\in B(w)
). Therefore, only
(2)
can be true. Then, since
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w^{\prime}
and
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
, we have that
(x,y)=(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
. But then Lemma
11.21
implies that
e=(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
, a contradiction. This shows that
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
.
∎

Lemma
11.28
suggests the following algorithm in order to find all Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cuts: for every vertex
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
, and every
u\in U_{1}(v)
, find the greatest proper ancestor
w
of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\geq w
, and then check whether
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
1

4
-cut using Lemma
11.27
.
This procedure is shown in Algorithm
28
. The proof of correctness and linear complexity is given in Proposition
11.29
.

foreach

vertex
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot

do

1

compute the set
U_{1}(v)

2

end foreach

3

foreach

vertex
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot

do

4

foreach

u\in U_{1}(v)

do

5

let
w
be the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
and
M(w)=M(v)

6

if

\mathit{low}(u)<w

and

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1

then

7

mark
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))\}

Compute all Type-3
\beta ii
-

Proposition 11.29
.

Algorithm
28
computes all Type-3
\beta ii
-
1

4
-cuts. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

Proof.

Let
C=\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
be a Type-3
\beta ii
-
1

4
-cut, where
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
. Then we have
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, and therefore
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Lemma
11.21
implies that
e=(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
and
\mathit{low}(u)<w
. Lemma
11.22
implies that
u\in U_{1}(v)
. Lemma
11.28
implies that
w
be the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
and
M(w)=M(v)
. Thus,
C
satisfies all the conditions to be marked in Line
28
.

Conversely, let
C=\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))\}
be a
4
-element set that is marked in Line
28
. Since
u\in U_{1}(v)
, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
w
is derived in Line
28
, we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
. Since the condition in Line
28
is satisfied, we have
\mathit{low}(u)<w
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Thus, all the conditions of Lemma
11.27
are satisfied, and therefore we have that there is a back-edge
e
such that
e\in B(u)\cap B(v)\cap B(w)
and
B(v)\setminus\{e\}=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. By the proof of Lemma
11.21
, we have
e=(\mathit{lowD}(u),\mathit{low}(u))
(this result is independent of the condition
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
that is implicit in the statement of this lemma). Thus, we have that
C
is a
4
-cut that satisfies
(1)
of Lemma
11.1
.

Now we will argue about the complexity of Algorithm
28
. By Lemma
11.25
we have that the sets
U_{1}(v)
can be computed in linear time in total, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. Thus, the
for
loop in Line
28
can be performed in linear time. In order to compute the vertex
w
in Line
28
we use Algorithm
12
. Specifically, whenever we reach Line
28
, we generate a query of the form
q(M^{-1}(M(v)),\mathit{min}\{p(v),\mathit{low}_{2}(u)\})
. This is to return the greatest
w
in
M^{-1}(M(v))
such that
w\leq p(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
. Since
M(w)=M(v)
,
w\leq p(v)
implies that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus,
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}_{2}(u)
. Since the number of all those queries is
O(n)
, Lemma
8.5
implies that they can be answered in linear time in total, using Algorithm
12
. We conclude that Algorithm
28
runs in linear time.
∎

11.2.2
Type-3
\beta ii
-
2

4
-cuts

Now we consider case
(2)
of Lemma
11.1
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(w)
such that
e\notin B(v)\cup B(u)
,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
M(v)=M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. By Lemma
11.1
, we have that
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
is a
4
-cut, and we call this a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut.

The following lemma provides some useful information concerning this type of
4
-cuts.

Lemma 11.30
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices such that
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, and let
e
be the back-edge of the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then
e
is either
(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
or
(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
. Furthermore,
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
,
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
,
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
,
\mathit{low}(v)<w
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Finally, if
u^{\prime}
is a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, then
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
,
M(v)=M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
,
e\in B(w)
and
e\notin B(v)\cup B(u)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that both
(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
and
(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
are back-edges in
B(v)
. Then
\mathit{nca}(L_{1}(w),R_{1}(w))
is a descendant of
M(v)
, which means that
M(w)
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Since
M(w)
is an ancestor of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
and
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
, we have that
M(w)
is an ancestor of
M(v)
. Thus we have that
M(w)=M(v)
. Since
w
is an ancestor of
v
, this implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
, which implies that
e\in B(v)
, a contradiction. Thus we have that at least one of
(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
and
(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
is not in
B(v)
. Due to
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
, we have that
e
is the only back-edge in
B(w)
that cannot be in
B(v)
, and therefore this coincides with either
(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
or
(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
. Observe that in the argument that we used we arrived at a contradiction from
M(w)=M(v)
. Thus,
M(w)\neq M(v)
, and therefore
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
.

Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this shows that
\mathit{high}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a back-edge
(x,y)
in
B(v)
such that
y>\mathit{high}(u)
. This implies that
(x,y)\notin B(u)
. Thus,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)
, which implies that
y<w
. Then
y>\mathit{high}(u)
implies that
\mathit{high}(u)<w
. Now let
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Furthermore, we have
y^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(u)<w
. Since
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
is a back-edge, we have that
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
y^{\prime}
. Thus,
x^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
y^{\prime}
and
w
, and therefore
y^{\prime}
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant, and therefore
y^{\prime}<w
implies that
y^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
w
. This shows that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(w)
, which is impossible, since
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. Thus we have that every back-edge
(x,y)\in B(v)
has
y\leq\mathit{high}(u)
, and therefore
\mathit{high}(v)\leq\mathit{high}(u)
. This shows that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
.

Since both
w
and
\mathit{high}(v)
are ancestors of
v
, we have that
w
and
\mathit{high}(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w
is a proper descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{high}(u)
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
y=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Furthermore,
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Thus we have
(x,y)\in B(w)
, contradicting
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. This shows that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
.

Since
u
is a descendant of
w
such that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w
. Since
B(w)\setminus\{e\}
is not empty,
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(v)\cap B(w)
, and therefore
y<w
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(v)<w
.

Now let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
u
is a descendant of
v
and
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is also a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
u\geq u^{\prime}
, we have that either
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
, or it is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u^{\prime}
is not an ancestor of
u
. Then
u^{\prime}
is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
with
y=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Thus,
y=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
implies that
(x,y)
is in
B(v)
. Since
u^{\prime}
is not related as ancestor and descendant with
u
, we have that
x
is not a descendant of
u
. Thus,
(x,y)\notin B(u)
. Now
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. But
y=\mathit{high}(v)
and
\mathit{high}(v)
is a descendant of
w
, a contradiction. This shows that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.
∎

According to Lemma
11.30
, if a triple of vertices
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, then the back-edge
e
of this
4
-cut is either
(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
or
(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
. In the following we will show how to handle the case where
e=(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
. To be specific, we will provide an algorithm that computes a collection of Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
, where
e=(L_{1}(w),l(L_{1}(w)))
, so that all
4
-cuts of this form are implied from this collection, plus that returned by Algorithm
14
. The algorithms, the propositions and the arguments for the case
e=(R_{1}(w),l(R_{1}(w)))
are similar. Thus, in this section, for every triple
(u,v,w)
that we consider that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, we assume that
e=e_{L}(w)
.

For convenience, we distinguish two cases of Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cuts. First, we have the case where
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. In this case, we compute only a subcollection of the
4
-cuts, which, together with the collection of Type-
2ii

4
-cuts returned by Algorithm
14
, implies all the Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cuts of this type (see Proposition
11.41
). Then we have the case where
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. In this case we can compute all those Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cuts in linear time explicitly (see Proposition
11.48
).

The case where
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, and let
e
be the back-edge of this
4
-cut. Then we have
e\in B(w)
and
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
. Furthermore, by Lemma
11.30
we have that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Now, for every vertex
v\neq r
, let
W(v)
be the collection of all vertices
w\neq r
such that:
(1)

M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})\neq M(w)
,
(2)

M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, and
(3)

L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. In particular, if
W(v)\neq\emptyset
, then we define
\mathit{firstW}(v)=\mathit{max}(W(v))
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)=\mathit{min}(W(v))
.

Lemma 11.31
.

Let
v
and
w
be two vertices such that
w\in W(v)
. Then
w
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
. Thus,
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
(x,y)\in B(w)
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
w
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
and
w
, and therefore
\mathit{high}(v)
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, we have that
w
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Then, since
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
w
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
w\in W(v)
. This shows that
w
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
.
∎

We will show how to compute the values
\mathit{firstW}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)
, for all vertices
v
. With those values we can determine in constant time whether
W(v)\neq\emptyset
, for a vertex
v
, by simply checking whether
\mathit{firstW}(v)\neq\bot
. First, for every vertex
x
, we let
W_{0}(x)
denote the list of all vertices
w\neq r
with
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
, sorted in decreasing order. Notice that, for every vertex
v\neq r
, we have
W(v)\subseteq W_{0}(M(v))
. Now we have the following.

Lemma 11.32
.

Let
v
be a vertex such that
W(v)\neq\emptyset
. Then
\mathit{lastW}(v)
is the last entry in
W_{0}(M(v))
.

Proof.

Let
w=\mathit{lastW}(v)
, and let
w^{\prime}
be the last entry in
W_{0}(M(v))
. Thus, we have
w^{\prime}\leq w
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}\neq w
. Since
w=\mathit{lastW}(v)
, we have that
w
is the lowest vertex in
W_{0}(M(v))
such that
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
w^{\prime}\neq w
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
w\in W_{0}(M(v))
, we have that
M(v)=M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})\neq M(w)
. Thus,
e_{L}(w)
is the only back-edge in
B(w)
whose higher endpoint (i.e.,
L_{1}(w)
) is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Similarly, since
w^{\prime}\in W_{0}(M(v))
, we have that
e_{L}(w^{\prime})
is the only back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
whose higher endpoint (i.e.,
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
) is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Notice that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
. This implies that
M(v)
is a common descendant of
w
and
w^{\prime}
, and therefore
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}\leq w
implies that
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
w
.

Since
w=\mathit{lastW}(v)
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)=e_{L}(w^{\prime})
. This implies that
x=L_{1}(w^{\prime})
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Since
(x,y)=e_{L}(w^{\prime})
, we have that
x
is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Thus, since
(x,y)
is a back-edge in
B(w)
such that
x
is not a descendant of
M(v)
, we have that
(x,y)=e_{L}(w)
. But this contradicts the fact that
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. We conclude that
w^{\prime}=w
.
∎

Lemma 11.33
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices with
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Suppose that
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
. Then
\mathit{firstW}(v)\neq\bot
, and
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{firstW}(v)
.

Proof.

Let
w=\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. Then we have that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v^{\prime})
and
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Since
v^{\prime}\neq v
and the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have that
B(v)\neq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
v
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
with
M(v)=M(v^{\prime})
, Lemma
6.6
implies that
v^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, this implies that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This shows that
w\in W(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{firstW}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{firstW}(v)\geq w
.
∎

Using the information provided by Lemmata
11.32
and
11.33
, we can provide an efficient algorithm for computing the values
\mathit{firstW}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)
, for all vertices
v
. First, for every vertex
x
, we collect all vertices
w\neq r
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
into a list
W_{0}(x)
, and we have
W_{0}(x)
sorted in decreasing order. The computation of the values
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
, for all
w\neq r
, takes linear time in total, according to Proposition
6.20
. Then, the construction of the lists
W_{0}(x)
takes
O(n)
time in total, using bucket-sort. Now, for every vertex
v\neq r
, it is sufficient to check the last entry
w
in
W_{0}(M(v))
in order to see if
w=\mathit{lastW}(v)
, according to Lemma
11.32
. Since
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, we have that
w\in W(v)
if and only if
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. So this can be easily checked in constant time.

In order to compute the values
\mathit{firstW}
, we traverse the lists
M^{-1}(x)
and
W_{0}(x)
simultaneously, for every vertex
x
. To be specific, let
v\neq r
be a vertex. Then, if
w=\mathit{firstW}(v)
exists, we have that
w\in W_{0}(M(v))
. (Notice that
v
itself lies in
M^{-1}(M(v))
.) Then, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus, it is sufficient to reach the greatest
w^{\prime}
in
W_{0}(M(v))
that is a proper ancestor of
v
. Then, as long as
w^{\prime}
does not satisfy the property that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we keep traversing the list
W_{0}(M(v))
. Eventually we will reach
w
. Now, if there is a proper ancestor
v^{\prime}
of
v
with
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
such that
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, then by Lemma
11.33
we have that
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. Thus, it is sufficient to pick up the search for
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
in
W_{0}(M(v^{\prime}))
from the last entry in
W_{0}(M(v^{\prime}))
that we accessed. This procedure for computing the values
\mathit{firstW}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)
