Lemma 11.34
.

Algorithm
29
correctly computes the values
\mathit{firstW}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)
, for all vertices
v
, in total linear time. If for a vertex
v
we have
W(v)=\emptyset
, then
\mathit{firstW}(v)=\bot
.

Recall that, for every vertex
x
, we let
H(x)
denote the list of all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{high}(v)=x
, sorted in decreasing order. Then, for every vertex
v\neq r
, we let
S(v)
denote the segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Furthermore, we let
U(v)
denote the subsegment of
S(v)
that contains all the proper descendants of
v
.
Now, for every vertex
v
such that
W(v)\neq\emptyset
, we let
U_{2}(v)
be the collection of all
u\in U(v)
such that: either
(1)

\mathit{firstW}(v)>\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
, or
(2)

u
is the lowest vertex in
U(v)
such that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
.

Lemma 11.35
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, where
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Then
u\in U_{2}(v)
and
w\in W(v)
.

Proof.

Let
e
be the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Due to our assumption in this subsection, we have that
e=e_{L}(w)
. Furthermore, we have
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
, and Lemma
11.30
implies that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Thus, since
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
,
w
satisfies all the conditions to be in
W(v)
.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, Lemma
11.30
implies that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. In other words, we have
u\in H(\mathit{high}(v))
. Now let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
u^{\prime}\in H(\mathit{high}(v))
. This means that we have
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore Lemma
11.30
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. This shows that
u\in S(v)
. Since
u
is a proper descendant of
v
, this implies that
u\in U(v)
.

Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
w\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
. By Lemma
11.30
we have
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus,
w\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
implies that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
. If
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{firstW}(v)
, then by definition we have
u\in U_{2}(v)
, and the proof is complete. Otherwise, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u^{\prime}\in U(v)
that is lower than
u
and satisfies
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U(v)
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
, and so we have
u^{\prime}>v
. Furthermore, since
u^{\prime}\in U(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
and
u>u^{\prime}>v
, by Lemma
11.30
we have that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, by Lemma
6.3
we have that
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(u)\subset B(u^{\prime})
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})\setminus B(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore it is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then, since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
. Since
(x,y)\notin B(u)
, this implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
w\leq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. But we have supposed that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq w
, which implies that
y\geq w
(since
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\leq y
). This means that
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, in contradiction to the fact that
(x,y)\in B(w)
.
This shows that
u
is the lowest vertex in
U(v)
that has
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. Thus, by definition, we have
u\in U_{2}(v)
.
∎

Lemma 11.36
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, where
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Let
w^{\prime}
be the greatest vertex in
W(v)
that has
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Then
(u,v,w^{\prime})
also induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut. Furthermore, if
w^{\prime}\neq w
, then
B(w)\sqcup\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}=B(w^{\prime})\sqcup\{e_{L}(w)\}
.

Proof.

By the assumption throughout this subsection, we have that the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
is
e=e_{L}(w)
. By Lemma
11.35
we have that
w\in W(v)
, and by Lemma
11.30
we have that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus, we may consider the greatest vertex
w^{\prime}
in
W(v)
that has
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. We will assume that
w^{\prime}\neq w
, because otherwise there is nothing to show.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
. Since
w^{\prime}\in W(v)
, we have
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore, since
w^{\prime}\in W(v)
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus we have that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, we have that
B(u)\cap B(w^{\prime})=\emptyset
. Thus, we have that
(x,y)\notin B(u)
, and therefore
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
, this shows that
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
w^{\prime}\in W(v)
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, we have that
x
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Since
w
and
w^{\prime}
are both in
W(v)
, Lemma
11.31
implies that they are both proper ancestors of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus,
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Due to the maximality of
w^{\prime}
, we have that
w^{\prime}>w
, and therefore
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
. Then, since
(x,y)\in B(w)
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. Since
x
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
, this shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Since
w^{\prime}\in W(v)
, we have that the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
x
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
(x,y)\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime})
, and therefore
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
. Thus we have shown that
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
. This implies that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e\})
is equivalent to
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})
, and therefore, by Lemma
11.1
,
(u,v,w^{\prime})
induces a
4
-cut. By definition, this is a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e_{L}(w^{\prime})=e_{L}(w)
. Then, since
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
, we have that
B(w^{\prime})=B(w)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, we have
e_{L}(w^{\prime})\neq e_{L}(w)
. Therefore,
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}=B(w)\setminus\{e\}
implies that
B(w)\sqcup\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}=B(w^{\prime})\sqcup\{e_{L}(w)\}
.
∎

Lemma 11.37
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices with
W(v)\neq\emptyset
and
W(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
such that
v
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
and
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Then
\mathit{lastW}(v)>\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

Let
w
and
w^{\prime}
be two vertices such that
w\in W(v)
and
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
. Then it is sufficient to show that
w>w^{\prime}
(because
\mathit{lastW}(v)=\mathit{min}(W(v))
and
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{max}(W(v^{\prime}))
). So let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w\leq w^{\prime}
. Since
v
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
with
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
M(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
M(v)
. But we cannot have that
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
, because the graph is
3
-edge-connected (and otherwise,
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
would imply
B(v)=B(v^{\prime})
, by Lemma
6.7
). Thus,
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. Notice that we cannot have
w=w^{\prime}
, because
w\in W(v)
and
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
imply that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
and
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v^{\prime})
(and we showed that we cannot have
M(v)=M(v^{\prime})
). Thus, we have
w<w^{\prime}
. Since
w\in W(v)
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. And since
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Thus,
v^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
w
and
w^{\prime}
, and therefore
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w<w^{\prime}
implies that
w
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
.

Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that all back-edges in
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
have their higher endpoint in
T(M(v^{\prime}))
. (We note that
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
is not empty, since the graph is
3
-edge-connected.) Then we have that
M(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, contradicting the fact that
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. This shows that there is at least one back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
such that
x
is not a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Since
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Therefore,
x
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, it cannot be the case that
(x,y)=e_{L}(w^{\prime})
(because
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
implies that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
). Now, since
x
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, and
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
(by Lemma
11.31
), we have that
x
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. But since
(x,y)\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime})
, we have that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
. Thus, since
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
, we have that
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, contradicting the fact that
x
is not a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. We conclude that
w>w^{\prime}
. Due to the generality of
w\in W(v)
and
w^{\prime}\in W(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
\mathit{lastW}(v)>\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Lemma 11.38
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices with
W(v)\neq\emptyset
and
W(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
. Suppose that
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to the same segment
S
of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. If
U_{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{2}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{2}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{2}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{2}(v)
, but
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
is empty. Since
u\in U_{2}(v)
we have that
u\in S
, and therefore
u
is related as ancestor and descendant with
v^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Since
W(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
, there is a vertex
w\in W(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have that
|B(w)|>1
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Since
w\in W(v^{\prime})
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
u\in U_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, which is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)
, which is a proper ancestor of
u
. Since
x
is a descendant of
u
, this shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Therefore,
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
. Since
(x,y)\in B(w)
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
y<w
. Thus,
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
implies that
\mathit{low}(u)<w
. Now, Lemma
11.37
implies that
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastW}(v)
. Thus, since
w\leq\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
w<\mathit{lastW}(v)
. But then
\mathit{low}(u)<w
implies that
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{lastW}(v)
, in contradiction to
u\in U_{2}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition cannot be true, and therefore we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
.

Now let us gather the information we have concerning
u
. We know that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and it belongs to
S
. Furthermore, since
u\in U_{2}(v)
we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
, and by Lemma
11.37
we have that
\mathit{lastW}(v)>\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v^{\prime}
in
S
that has
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
, and so
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
cannot be empty. A contradiction. Thus, we have shown that
U_{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
implies that
U_{2}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{2}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be any vertex in
U_{2}(v)
, and let
u^{\prime}
be any vertex in
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u<u^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{2}(v)
, we have that
u\in S
. And since
u^{\prime}\in U_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}\in S
. Thus,
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Therefore,
u<u^{\prime}
implies that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that either
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
, or
u^{\prime}
is the lowest proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
S
such that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
.

Let us suppose, first, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. Since
u
is an ancestor of
u^{\prime}
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
(since
u
and
u^{\prime}
are in
S
), by Lemma
6.3
we have that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Therefore,
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
implies that
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. Lemma
11.37
implies that
\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastW}(v)
. Therefore, we have
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{lastW}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{2}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition cannot be true, and therefore we have that
u^{\prime}
is the lowest proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
S
such that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
. Now, since
u\in U_{2}(v)
, we can argue as above in order to establish that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the argument above did not make use of the assumption
U_{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, and so it can be applied here too). But then, since
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
S
such that
u<u^{\prime}
, the minimality of
u^{\prime}
implies that
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{firstW}(v^{\prime})
, and so we can arrive again at
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{lastW}(v)
, in contradiction to
u\in U_{2}(v)
. This shows that
u\geq u^{\prime}
. Due to the generality of
u\in U_{2}(v)
, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{2}(v)
is at least as great as
u^{\prime}
. And due to the generality of
u^{\prime}\in U_{2}(v^{\prime})
, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{2}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Based on Lemma
11.38
, we can provide an efficient algorithm for computing the sets
U_{2}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
W(v)\neq\emptyset
. The computation takes place on segments of
H(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Specifically, let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
W(v)\neq\emptyset
. Then we have that
U_{2}(v)\subset S(v)
. In other words,
U_{2}(v)
is a subset of the segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. So let
z_{1},\dots,z_{k}
be the vertices of
S(v)
, sorted in decreasing order. Then, we have that
v=z_{i}
, for an
i\in\{1,\dots,k\}
. By definition,
U_{2}(v)
contains every vertex
u
in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
such that either
\mathit{firstW}(v)>\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in this set such that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW}(v)
. As an implication of Lemma
6.5
, we have that the vertices in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
are sorted in decreasing order w.r.t. their
\mathit{low}
point. Thus, it is sufficient to process the vertices from
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
in reverse order, in order to find the first vertex
u
that has
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW}(v)
. Then, we keep traversing this set in reverse order, and, as long as the
\mathit{low}
point of every vertex
u
that we meet is lower than
\mathit{firstW}(v)
, we insert
u
into
U_{2}(v)
. Then, once we reach a vertex with
\mathit{low}
point no lower than
\mathit{firstW}(v)
, we also insert it into
U_{2}(v)
, and we are done.

Now, if there is a proper ancestor
v^{\prime}
of
v
in
S(v)
such that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, then we have that
S(v)=S(v^{\prime})
. If
W(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
, then we have that
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
is defined. Then we can follow the same process as above in order to compute
U_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, according to Lemma
11.38
, it is sufficient to start from the greatest element of
U_{2}(v)
(i.e., the one that was inserted last into
U_{2}(v)
). In particular, if
U_{2}(v)=\emptyset
, then it is certain that
U_{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, and therefore we are done. Otherwise, we just pick up the computation from the greatest vertex in
U_{2}(v)
. In order to perform efficiently those computations, first we compute, for every vertex
x
, the collection
\mathcal{S}(x)
of the segments of
H(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. For every vertex
x
, this computation takes
O(|H(x)|)
time using Algorithm
11
, according to Lemma
6.25
. Since every vertex
\neq r
participates in exactly one set of the form
H(x)
, we have that the total size of all
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for all vertices
x
, is
O(n)
. Then it is sufficient to process separately all segments of
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for every vertex
x
, as described above, by starting the computation each time from the first vertex
v
of the segment that satisfies
W(v)\neq\emptyset
. The whole procedure is shown in Algorithm
30
. The result is formally stated in Lemma
11.39
.

Lemma 11.39
.

Algorithm
30
correctly computes the sets
U_{2}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
W(v)\neq\emptyset
. Furthermore, it runs in linear time.

Proof.

The idea behind Algorithm
30
and its correctness has been discussed in the main text above.
It is easy to see that Algorithm
30
runs in
O(n)
time, provided that we have computed the vertices
\mathit{firstW}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW}(v)
for every vertex
v
(if they exist). This can be achieved in linear time according to Lemma
11.34
. Thus, Algorithm
30
has a linear-time implementation.
∎

Lemma 11.40
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices such that
u\in U_{2}(v)
,
w\in W(v)
,
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Then,
e_{L}(w)\notin B(u)\cup B(v)
, and
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
.

Proof.

Since
u\in U_{2}(v)
we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Since
w\in W(v)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Since
w\in W(v)
, by Lemma
11.31
we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
, this implies that
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}\subseteq B(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
, and therefore
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
implies that
w\leq y
. Thus,
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
(x,y)\notin B(w)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this shows that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. Now, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
and
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}\subseteq B(v)
and
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
. Furthermore, since
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, we have that
e_{L}(w)\notin B(u)
, and therefore
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
implies that
e_{L}(w)\notin B(v)
. Thus, we have
e_{L}(w)\notin B(u)\cup B(v)
.
∎

Now let

The case where
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)

Lemma 11.42
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, where
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Then
w
is the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Proof.

Let
e
be the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. By the assumption we have made for the
4
-cuts in this subsection, we have that
e=e_{L}(w)
. Then, by Lemma
11.30
we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
,
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is an ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
\mathit{high}(v)
with
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, such that
w^{\prime}>w
. Since
w^{\prime}
and
w
have
\mathit{high}(v)
as a common descendant, they are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}>w
implies that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
.

Since
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore, the lower endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
e_{L}(w)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Since
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, we have that
e_{L}(w)
is the only back-edge in
B(w)
whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Similarly, since
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
, we have that
e_{L}(w^{\prime})
is the only back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Thus, since
e_{L}(w)\in B(w^{\prime})
, we have
e_{L}(w)=e_{L}(w^{\prime})
.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
. This implies that
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}=B(v)\setminus B(u)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)
. If
(x,y)=e_{L}(w)
, then
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Otherwise,
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}=B(v)\setminus B(u)
implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Therefore,
x
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
. If
(x,y)=e_{L}(w^{\prime})
, then
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Otherwise,
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, we have that
B(u)\cap B(w^{\prime})=\emptyset
(because no back-edge in
B(u)
has low enough lower endpoint in order to leap over
w^{\prime}
). Thus, we have
(x,y)\notin B(u)
, and therefore
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus B(u)
. Since
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}=B(v)\setminus B(u)
, this implies that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. Thus, we have that
B(w^{\prime})=B(w)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. We conclude that
w
is the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.
∎

Lemma
11.42
motivates the following definition. Let
v
be a vertex
\neq r
. Then we let
\widetilde{W}(v)
denote the collection of all vertices
w
such that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
,
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and

. Then, Lemma

implies that, if there is a triple of vertices

that induces a Type-3
\beta

2

4
-cut such that

is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, then

. Thus, the sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
can guide us into the search for such
4
-cuts.

Lemma 11.43
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two distinct vertices
\neq r
. Then
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
.

Proof.

If
M(v)\neq M(v^{\prime})
, then obviously
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
. (Because every vertex
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
has
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, and every vertex
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
has
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v^{\prime})
.) Thus, we may assume that
M(v)=M(v^{\prime})
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Since
v\neq v^{\prime}
, we may assume w.l.o.g. that
v>v^{\prime}
. Therefore, since
v
and
v^{\prime}
have
M(v)=M(v^{\prime})
as a common descendant, we have that
v
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Let
w
be a vertex in
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Furthermore, since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Notice that, since
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
(i.e., the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
) is not a descendant of
M(v)
. Since
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
, by Lemma
6.2
we have that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{high}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
, this implies that
B(v)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
implies that
B(v)=B(v^{\prime})
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, we have that
\mathit{high}(v)
is not a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Since
\mathit{high}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and
v^{\prime}
is also an ancestor of
v
, we have that
\mathit{high}(v)
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
\mathit{high}(v)
is not a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
\mathit{high}(v)
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
.

Now, since
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, it is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore, since
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Therefore, the lower endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
(since it is a proper ancestor of
w
). This shows that
e_{L}(w)\in B(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. But
L_{1}(w)
is not a descendant of
M(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
. Thus, we conclude that
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
.
∎

Lemma 11.44
.

For every vertex
x
, let
\widetilde{L}(x)
be the list of all
w
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
, sorted in decreasing order. Let
v
be a vertex such that
M(v)=x
and
\widetilde{W}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Let
w=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
. Then,
w
is the greatest vertex in
\widetilde{L}(x)
such that
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Furthermore,
\widetilde{W}(v)
is a segment of
\widetilde{L}(x)
.

Proof.

By definition of
\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
w=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
with
w^{\prime}>w
, such that
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
, we have that
w^{\prime}
and
w
have
x
as a common descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant. Therefore,
w^{\prime}>w
implies that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
.

Since
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
, we have that
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=x=M(v)
. Thus, since
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
and
M(v)
is a descendant of
v
, we have that
w^{\prime}
and
v
have
x
as a common descendant, and therefore they are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(v)
and
\mathit{high}(v)
is an ancestor of
v
, we have that
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
v
. Thus, since
w^{\prime}
and
\mathit{high}(v)
have
v
as a common descendant, we have that
w^{\prime}
is related as ancestor and descendant with
\mathit{high}(v)
. Therefore,
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(v)
implies that
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
w=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
and
w^{\prime}>w
, we have that
w^{\prime}\notin\widetilde{W}(v)
. Thus, since
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
(because this is the only condition that prevents
w^{\prime}
to be in
\widetilde{W}(v)
). Notice that, since
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=x
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
(i.e., the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(w^{\prime})
) is not a descendant of
x
.

Since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus,
e_{L}(w)\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime})
. Since
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. And since the lower endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
is a proper ancestor of
w
, we have that the lower endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
e_{L}(w)\in B(w^{\prime})
. Notice that, since
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
, we have that
L_{1}(w)
(i.e., the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(w)
) is not a descendant of
x
. Since
e_{L}(w)\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime})
and
e_{L}(w)\in B(w^{\prime})
, we have that
e_{L}(w)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
. Thus,
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
contains a back-edge whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
x
, and therefore
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})\neq x
, a contradiction. Thus, we have shown that there is no vertex
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
with
w^{\prime}>w
, such that
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. This shows that
w
is the greatest vertex in
\widetilde{L}(x)
such that
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
.

By definition, we have that
\widetilde{W}(v)\subseteq\widetilde{L}(x)
. (Since
\widetilde{L}(x)
contains every vertex
w
such that
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
.) Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\widetilde{W}(v)
is not a segment of
\widetilde{L}(x)
. Since
w=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
, this means that there are
w^{\prime}
and
w^{\prime\prime}
in
\widetilde{L}(x)
, with
w>w^{\prime}>w^{\prime\prime}
, such that
w^{\prime}\notin\widetilde{W}(v)
and
w^{\prime\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v)
. Since
w,w^{\prime},w^{\prime\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(B(w^{\prime\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})\})=x
. Thus,
\{w,w^{\prime},w^{\prime\prime}\}
have
x
as a common descendant, and therefore all three of them are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w>w^{\prime}>w^{\prime\prime}
implies that
w
is a proper descendant of
w^{\prime}
, and
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w^{\prime\prime}
.

Since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This implies that
w^{\prime}
is also an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
and
w^{\prime}\notin\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Now, since
w^{\prime\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus,
e_{L}(w^{\prime})\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})
. Since
L_{1}(w^{\prime\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
and
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
L_{1}(w^{\prime\prime})
is a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore, the lower endpoint of
e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})\in B(w^{\prime})
. As previously, notice that
e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})
is not a descendant of
x
(since
M(w^{\prime\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})\})=x
). Since
e_{L}(w^{\prime})\neq e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})
and
e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})\in B(w^{\prime})
, we have that
e_{L}(w^{\prime\prime})\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
. Thus,
B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\}
contains a back-edge whose higher endpoint is not a descendant of
x
, and therefore
M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})\neq x
– in contradiction to
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{L}(x)
. Thus, we conclude that
\widetilde{W}(v)
is a segment of
\widetilde{L}(x)
.
∎

Algorithm
32
shows how we can compute all sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
, for all
v\neq r
, in total linear time. The idea is to find, for every vertex
v
, the greatest
w
that has
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. According to Lemma
11.44
, if
\widetilde{W}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then this
w
must satisfy
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
(i.e., it also has that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
). Then, still according to Lemma
11.44
, we have that
\widetilde{W}(v)
is a segment of the decreasingly sorted list that consists of all vertices
w^{\prime}
with
M(w^{\prime})\neq M(B(w^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(w^{\prime})\})=M(v)
. Thus, we keep traversing this list, and we greedily insert as many vertices as we can into
\widetilde{W}(v)
, until we reach a
w^{\prime}
that no longer satisfies that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
.
The full proof of correctness and linear complexity of Algorithm
32
is given in Lemma
11.45
. The proof of linear complexity relies on Lemma
11.43
: i.e., the sets in
\{\widetilde{W}(v)\mid v\mbox{ is a vertex }\neq r\}
are pairwise disjoint.

compute

, for every
w\neq r

\widetilde{L}(x)\leftarrow\emptyset
, for every vertex
x

2

w\leftarrow n
to
w=2

then

4

\widetilde{L}(M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}))

5

6

7

//

w

, sorted in decreasing order, for every vertex

Algorithm 32

Compute the sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
, for all
v\neq r

Lemma 11.45
.

Algorithm
32
correctly computes the sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

Proof.

It should be clear that, when we reach Line
32
, we have that
\widetilde{L}(x)
, for every vertex
x
, is the decreasingly sorted list of all vertices
w
that have
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=x
. The idea in the
for
loop in Line
32
is to process all vertices
v\neq r
in a bottom-up fashion. Then, for every vertex
v\neq r
, we start searching in
\widetilde{L}(M(v))
for the greatest vertex
w
that has
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
(see the
while
loop in Line
32
). This search for this
w
starts from the last vertex that we accessed in
\widetilde{L}(M(v))
. This is ensured by the use of variable
\mathit{currentVertex}[x]
(where
x=M(v)
), which we use in order to initialize
w
in Line
32
, and then we update
\mathit{currentVertex}[x]
in Line
32
. We only have to explain why this is sufficient.

First, we have that, if
v^{\prime}
and
v
are two vertices with
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
and
v^{\prime}<v
, then
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. To see this, suppose the contrary. Since
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
, we have that
v^{\prime}
and
v
have
M(v)
as a common descendant. Therefore,
v^{\prime}<v
implies that
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}(v)
is also a proper ancestor of
v
, we have that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{high}(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then, since
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is not an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
, it must be a proper descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}(v)\geq\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, a contradiction. Therefore, we have indeed that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{high}(v)
.

Now we can see inductively that
\widetilde{W}(v)
is computed correctly by the
for
loop in Line
32
, for every vertex
v\neq r
. We use induction on the number of times that a vertex
v
with
M(v)=x
is processed, for every fixed
x
. The first time that the
for
loop in Line
32
processes a vertex
v
with
M(v)=x
, we begin the search for vertices
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
from the beginning of
\widetilde{L}(x)
(due to the initialization of
\mathit{currentVertex}[x]
in Line
32
). The
while
loop in Line
32
traverses the list
\widetilde{L}(x)
, until it reaches a vertex
w
such that
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, this is the greatest vertex in
\widetilde{L}(x)
such that
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. According to Lemma
11.44
, if
\widetilde{W}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then
w=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
. Since
w\in\widetilde{L}(x)
and
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
, it is sufficient to check whether
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. If that is the case, then we correctly insert
w
into
\widetilde{W}(v)
, in Line
32
. Furthermore, by Lemma
11.44
we have that
\widetilde{W}(v)
is a segment of
\widetilde{L}(x)
. Thus, since
w
is the leftmost element of this segment, it is sufficient to keep traversing
\widetilde{L}(x)
, and keep inserting all the vertices that we meet into
\widetilde{W}(v)
, until we meet a vertex that is provably no longer in
\widetilde{W}(v)
. Since
\widetilde{L}(x)
is sorted in decreasing order, all the vertices
w^{\prime}
that we meet have
w^{\prime}\leq w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, the only reason that may prevent such a
w^{\prime}
to be in
\widetilde{W}(v)
, is that
L_{1}(w^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. This shows that the
while
loop in Line
32
will correctly compute
\widetilde{W}(v)
. Then, in Line
32
we set “
\mathit{currentVertex}[x]\leftarrow w
”. This implies that the next time that we meet a vertex
v^{\prime}
that has
M(v^{\prime})=x
, we will start the search for
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
from the last entry
w
of
\widetilde{L}(x)
that we accessed while processing
v
. This is sufficient for the following reasons. First, since the
for
loop in Line
32
processes the vertices in a bottom-up fashion, we have that the next
v^{\prime}
with
M(v^{\prime})=x
that it will process is a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus, as shown above, we have that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Then, the search from
\widetilde{L}(x)
will be picked up from the vertex
w
that is either the greatest that satisfies
w\leq\mathit{high}(v)
, or it is the lowest in
\widetilde{W}(v)
. In the first case, it is sufficient to start the search in
\widetilde{L}(x)
for
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
from
w
. In the second case, we note that by Lemma
11.43
we have that
\widetilde{W}(v)\cap\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
. Thus, no vertex that is greater than
w
can be in
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
: because no vertex in
\widetilde{W}(v)
is in
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
, and by Lemma
11.44
we have that the greatest vertex in
\widetilde{W}(v)
is the greatest vertex
w^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{L}(x)
that has
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, with the same argument that we used for
v
we can see that
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
will be correctly computed, and the same is true for any future vertex
v^{\prime\prime}
with
M(v^{\prime\prime})=x
that we will meet. This demonstrates the correctness of Algorithm
32
.

By Proposition
6.20
, we have that the values
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
, for all vertices
w\neq r
, can be computed in linear time in total. Thus, Line
32
can be performed in linear time. All other steps take
O(n)
time in total. In particular, observe that, in the worst case, the
for
loop in Line
32
may have to traverse the entire lists
M^{-1}(x)
and
\widetilde{L}(x)
, for all vertices
x
. Still, since all lists
M^{-1}(x)
are pairwise disjoint, and all lists
\widetilde{L}(x)
are pairwise disjoint, we have that the
for
loop in Line
32
takes
O(n)
time. Thus, Algorithm
32
runs in linear time.
∎

Lemma 11.46
.

A triple of vertices
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, where
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
, if and only if:
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
(2)

u
and
v
belong to a segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant,
(3)

w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
,
(4)

w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
(5)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
.

Proof.

(\Rightarrow)
Due to the convention we have made in this subsection, we have that the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
is
e_{L}(w)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut, by definition we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then, Lemma
11.30
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. Thus, the segment from
u
to
v
in
H(\mathit{high}(v))
consists of vertices that are related as ancestor and descendant (since all of them are ancestors of
u
). This implies
(2)
. Lemma
11.42
implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
and
M(w)\neq M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. By assumption we have that
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus,
w
satisfies all the conditions to be in
\widetilde{W}(v)
.
(4)
is an implication of Lemma
11.30
.
(5)
is an immediate implication of the fact that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
.

(\Leftarrow)

(2)
implies that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Since by
(1)
we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
. Since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})=M(v)
. Thus, since
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
(since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
). This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}
, this implies that
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}\subseteq B(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
. Therefore,
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
implies that
w\leq y
. Thus,
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
(x,y)\notin B(w)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. Thus, since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
and
B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\}\subseteq B(v)
and
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
. Thus,
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut.
∎

Lemma 11.47
.

Let
u
and
v
be two distinct vertices with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
that are related as ancestor and descendant. Then,
\mathit{bcount}(u)\neq\mathit{bcount}(v)
.

Proof.

We may assume w.l.o.g. that
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Thus, if we suppose that
\mathit{bcount}(u)=\mathit{bcount}(v)
, then we have that
B(u)=B(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. This shows that
\mathit{bcount}(u)\neq\mathit{bcount}(v)
.
∎

Now we will show how to compute all Type-3

. So let

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Then, Lemma

\mathit{bcount}(u)=\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
. Thus, the idea is to process separately all segments of

. Let

(u,v,w)
induces a

. The proof of correctness and linear complexity is given in Proposition
11.48
.

Algorithm 33

Compute all Type-3
\beta

2

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(w)\}

Proposition 11.48
.

Algorithm
33
correctly computes all Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(w)\}
, where
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
and
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

Proof.

For every vertex
x
, let
\mathcal{S}(x)
be the collection of the segments of
H(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant.
Let
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(w)\}
be a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut such that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
and
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Lemma
11.46
implies that
u
and
v
belong to the same segment
S
of
\mathcal{S}(\mathit{high}(v))
,
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
,
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Let
x=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then, during the processing of
S\in\mathcal{S}(x)
(in the
for
loop in Line
33
), we will eventually reach Line
33
for this particular
w
(during the
for
loop in Line
33
). We will show that the
\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
entry of the
A
array is precisely
u
. Notice that the entries of
A
are filled with vertices in Line
33
, for every segment
S\in\mathcal{S}(x)
, for every vertex
x
. And then, after the processing of
S
, the entries of
A
that were filled with vertices are set again to
\mathit{null}
in Line
33
. Thus, when we reach Line
33
, we have that the non-
\mathit{null}
entries of
A
contain vertices from
S
. More precisely, for every
z\in S
, we have that
A[\mathit{bcount}(z)]=z
. Thus, since all vertices in
S
are related as ancestor and descendant and have the same
\mathit{high}
point, Lemma
11.47
implies that
A[\mathit{bcount}(z)]=z
, for every
z\in S
, when the
for
loop in Line
33
is completed (during the processing of
S
); and also, we have
A[c]=\bot
, if there is no vertex
z\in S
with
\mathit{bcount}(z)=c
. Therefore, since
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
\mathit{bcount}(u)=\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, and therefore
A[\mathit{bcount}(v)-\mathit{bcount}(w)+1]=u
. Thus, when we reach Line
33
, we have that the variable “u” contains the value
u
, and so the
4
-cut
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(w)\}
will be correctly marked in Line
33
(since the condition in Line
33
is satisfied).

Conversely, whenever the condition in Line
33
is satisfied, we have that:
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
(2)

u
and
v
belong to a segment of
H(\mathit{high}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant,
(3)

w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
,
(4)

w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
(5)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Thus, Lemma
11.46
implies that
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(w)\}
is a Type-3
\beta
ii-
2

4
-cut such that
B(v)=B(u)\sqcup(B(w)\setminus\{e_{L}(w)\})
and
L_{1}(w)
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)
. Therefore, it is correct to mark it in Line
33
.

Now let us establish the linear-time complexity of Algorithm
33
. First, by Lemma
11.45
we have that Line
33
has a linear-time implementation. In particular, Lemma
11.43
implies that the total size of all sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
, for
v\neq r
, is
O(n)
. Then, by Lemma
6.25
we have that the collections
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for every vertex
x
, can be computed in linear time in total. Thus, the
for
loop in Line
33
has a linear-time implementation. Finally, the
for
loop in Line
33
is completed in linear time, precisely because all segments in the collection
\{S\in\mathcal{S}(x)\mid x\mbox{ is a vertex }\}
are pairwise disjoint, and so they have total size
O(n)
, and the sets
\widetilde{W}(v)
, for all
v\neq r
, have total size
O(n)
.
∎

11.2.3
Type-3
\beta ii
-
3

4
-cuts

Now we consider case
(3)
of Lemma
11.1
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(u)
such that
e\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
,
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
and
M(w)=M(v)
. By Lemma
11.1
, we have that
C=\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
is a
4
-cut, and we call this a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut.

The following lemma provides some useful information concerning this type of
4
-cuts.

Lemma 11.49
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, and let
e
be the back-edge of this
4
-cut. Then
e=(\mathit{highD}(u),\mathit{high}(u))
. Furthermore,
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w
and
\mathit{high}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Finally, if
u^{\prime}
is a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and either
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
or
\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, then
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, we have that
e\in B(u)
,
e\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
, and
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)

(*)
. This implies that
e
is the only back-edge in
B(u)
that is not in
B(v)
. Now let
(x_{1},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{k},y_{k})
be all the back-edges in
B(u)
sorted in decreasing order w.r.t. their lower endpoint, so that we have
(x_{i},y_{i})=(\mathit{highD}_{i}(u),\mathit{high}_{i}(u))
, for every
i\in\{1,\dots,k\}
. Let
i\in\{1,\dots,k\}
be an index such that
(x_{i},y_{i})\in B(v)
. Then we have that
y_{i}
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This implies that all
y_{j}
, with
j\in\{i,\dots,k\}
are proper ancestors of
v
. Furthermore, we have that all
x_{j}
, for
j\in\{1,\dots,k\}
, are descendants of
u
, and therefore all of them are descendants of
v
. This shows that all the back-edges
(x_{i},y_{i}),\dots,(x_{k},y_{k})
are in
B(v)
. Thus, we cannot have that
(x_{1},y_{1})\in B(v)
, because otherwise we would have
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Since
e
is the unique back-edge in
B(u)\setminus B(v)
, this shows that
e=(x_{1},y_{1})
, and therefore
e=(\mathit{highD}(u),\mathit{high}(u))
. Furthermore, this argument also shows that
y_{2}\neq y_{1}
, and therefore
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
.

Since
e=(\mathit{highD}(u),\mathit{high}(u))
and
B(u)\setminus\{e\}\subseteq B(v)
(and
B(u)\setminus\{e\}
contains at least one back-edge, since the graph is
3
-edge-connected), we have that
(x_{2},y_{2})\in B(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{high}(v)\geq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
y=\mathit{high}(v)
. We can use a similar argument as above, in order to conclude that, if
\mathit{high}(v)<w
, then
B(v)\subseteq B(w)
. But this is impossible to be the case, since there are back-edges from
B(u)
in
B(v)
, and we have
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. Thus, we have that
(x,y)\notin B(w)
. Then
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
implies that
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e\}
. Since
e=(\mathit{highD}(u),\mathit{high}(u))
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
, this implies that
y_{2}\geq y
. Thus we have
\mathit{high}_{2}(u)\geq\mathit{high}(v)
. This shows that
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(u)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u)<w
. Consider a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Furthermore, since
\mathit{low}(u)<w
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
(because
y
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant, since both of them are ancestors of
u
). This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
. But this contradicts
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, which is a consequence of
(*)
. Thus we have shown that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w
.

Now let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex with
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
such that there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
with
y=\mathit{high}(v)
(notice that this includes the cases
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
). Since
u
is a descendant of
v
,
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
implies that
u^{\prime}
is a descendant of
v
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
v
. Thus, since
y=\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, by definition we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
. Then, Lemma
6.6
implies that
\mathit{high}(v)
is a descendant of
w
. Thus,
y=\mathit{high}(v)
is not a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
(x,y)\notin B(w)
. Thus,
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
implies that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Then we have that
x
is a common descendant of
u
and
u^{\prime}
, and therefore
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
u\geq u^{\prime}
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.
∎

Recall that, for every vertex
x
, we let
\widetilde{H}(x)
denote the list of all vertices
z
such that either
\mathit{high}_{1}(z)=x
or
\mathit{high}_{2}(z)=x
, sorted in decreasing order. For every vertex
v\neq r
, let
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
denote the segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Then, for every vertex
v\neq r
with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
, we let
U_{3}(v)
denote the collection of all
u\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
such that:
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
(2)

\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
,
(3)

\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and
(4)
either
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{nextM}(v)
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
that satisfies
(1)
,
(2)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

Lemma 11.50
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut. Then
U_{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
, and let
\tilde{u}
be the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
. Then, if
u\notin U_{3}(v)
, we have that
(\tilde{u},v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, and
B(\tilde{u})\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}=B(u)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
.

Proof.

Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex in
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}(v))
such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
. Since
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}(v))
, we have that either
\mathit{high}_{1}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
or
\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, by Lemma
11.49
we have that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. This implies that all vertices from
u
to
v
in
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}(v))
are related as ancestor and descendant (since all of them are ancestors of
u
). This shows that
u\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
. Furthermore, by Lemma
11.49
we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Thus, if
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{nextM}(v)
, then we have
u\in U_{3}(v)
. Otherwise, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, and therefore we have
U_{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
, because we can consider the lowest vertex
\tilde{u}\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
that is a proper descendant of
v
and satisfies
\mathit{high}_{1}(\tilde{u})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

This shows that
U_{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Furthermore, this shows that, if
u\notin U_{3}(v)
, then we can define
\tilde{u}
as previously, and we have
\tilde{u}<u
(due to the minimality of
\tilde{u}
), and therefore
\tilde{u}
is a proper ancestor of
u
(since both
\tilde{u}
and
u
are in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
, and therefore they are related as ancestor and descendant).
Now we will show that
\tilde{u}
is the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
. Notice that
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, and every other vertex
u^{\prime}\in U_{3}(v)
(except
\tilde{u}
, that is) satisfies
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v)
. So let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\tilde{u}
is not the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
. Thus, there is a vertex
u^{\prime}\in U_{3}(v)
such that
u^{\prime}>\tilde{u}
. Since both
u^{\prime}
and
\tilde{u}
are in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
, this implies that
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
\tilde{u}
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
\tilde{u}
. We also have
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v)\leq\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
x
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
is an ancestor of
\tilde{u}
, and therefore an ancestor of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore an ancestor of
x
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
y
and
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
, and therefore
y
and
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
are related as ancestor and descendant, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
(since
y<\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
). Since
x
is a descendant of
\tilde{u}
, this implies that
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})
. But
y
is lower than
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
, a contradiction. This shows that
\tilde{u}
is the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
.

Now let us assume that
u\notin U_{3}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})=e_{\mathit{high}}(u)
. Then, since
\tilde{u}
is an ancestor of
u
, by Lemma
6.3
we have
B(u)\subseteq B(\tilde{u})
. This can be strengthened to
B(u)\subset B(\tilde{u})
, since the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})\setminus B(u)
. In particular, we have
(x,y)\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(u)=e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})
. Since
\tilde{u}\in U_{3}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
(x,y)\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})
, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore it is a proper ancestor of
v
. Furthermore,
x
is a descendant of
\tilde{u}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then, since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut, we have
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
. Thus, since
(x,y)\in B(v)
and
(x,y)\notin B(u)
, we have
(x,y)\in B(w)
. But we have
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})\geq w
, and therefore
y\geq w
(since
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})
implies that
y\geq\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})
). Thus,
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, a contradiction. This shows that
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(u)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\in B(u)
. Since
\tilde{u}\in U_{3}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(\tilde{u})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}(v)
. This implies that the lower endpoint of
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})
is greater than
\mathit{high}(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)
is the only back-edge in
B(u)
whose lower endpoint is greater than
\mathit{high}(v)
. Thus, since
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\in B(u)
, we have
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})=e_{\mathit{high}}(u)
, a contradiction. This shows that
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\notin B(u)
. Similarly, we can show that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(\tilde{u})
.

Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
\tilde{u}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
\tilde{u}\in U_{3}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then,
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
. The case
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected, since
\mathit{low}(\tilde{u})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)\geq w
. Thus, we have
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
, this shows that
B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}\subseteq B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
\tilde{u}
. Furthermore, we have
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\tilde{u}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})
. Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
and
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\notin B(u)
, we have
(x,y)\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
, this shows that
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}\subseteq B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
. Thus, we have shown that
B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}=B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
.

Then, since
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\notin B(u)
and
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(\tilde{u})
, we have
B(\tilde{u})\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}=B(u)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\}
. Furthermore, since
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
, we have
B(v)=(B(\tilde{u})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\})\sqcup B(w)
. Finally, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(\tilde{u})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(\tilde{u})>\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore
e_{\mathit{high}}(\tilde{u})\notin B(v)
. Then, by Lemma
11.1
, we conclude that
(\tilde{u},v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
3

4
-cut.
∎

Lemma 11.51
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
and
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)=\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. If
U_{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{3}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{3}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
(if it exists) is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
and
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
, by Lemma
6.3
we have that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(v^{\prime})\subset B(v)
. This implies that
M(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, we cannot have
M(v^{\prime})=M(v)
, because otherwise Lemma
6.7
implies that
B(v^{\prime})=B(v)
. Thus, we have that
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. Since
\mathit{lastM}(v)
is an ancestor of
M(v)
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
M(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Since
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
and
M(\mathit{lastM}(v))=M(v)
, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(\mathit{lastM}(v))
such that
x
is not a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. By Lemma
6.9
, we have that
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Therefore, since
x
is a descendant of
\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime}))
. But
x
is not a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})=M(\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime}))
, a contradiction. Thus, we have that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Therefore, since
\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant, we have that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
and
U_{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be a vertex in
U_{3}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{3}(v)
, we have
u\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
. Since
v^{\prime}
is also in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
, this implies that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
. Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime}))\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus, we have that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
\mathit{low}(\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime}))
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, this implies that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now, since
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. But then we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{3}(v)
. Thus, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then, since
u\in U_{3}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)=\mathit{high}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
is not empty (because we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(u^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
). This contradicts our supposition that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Thus, we have shown that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
implies that
U_{3}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
is not empty. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{3}(v)
that is lower than the greatest vertex
u^{\prime}
in
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
.
Since
u\in U_{3}(v)
and
u^{\prime}\in U_{3}(v^{\prime})
, we have
u\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
and
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, respectively. Thus, since
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)=\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Thus, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{3}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
u^{\prime}\in U_{3}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, and
u^{\prime}
is the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(u^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
that has this property
(*)
.

Now we will trace the implications of
u\in U_{3}(v)
. First, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)=\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Then, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)>\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
(since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
). Finally, we can show as above that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the proof of this fact above did not rely on
U_{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
). But then, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have a contradiction to
(*)
.
Thus, we have shown that every vertex in
U_{3}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
. In particular, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Based on Lemma
11.51
, we can provide an efficient algorithm for computing the sets
U_{3}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. The computation takes place on segments of
\widetilde{H}(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Specifically, let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. Then we have
U_{3}(v)\subset\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
. In other words,
U_{3}(v)
is a subset of the segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. So let
z_{1},\dots,z_{k}
the vertices of
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
, sorted in decreasing order. Then, we have that
v=z_{i}
, for an
i\in\{1,\dots,k\}
. By definition,
U_{3}(v)
contains every vertex
u
in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
such that either
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
\mathit{nextM}(v)>\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in this set with
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
. As an implication of Lemma
6.27
, we have that the vertices in
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
are sorted in decreasing order w.r.t. their
\mathit{low}
point. Thus, it is sufficient to process the vertices from
\{z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}\}
in reverse order, in order to find the first vertex
u
that has
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Then, we keep traversing this set in reverse order, and, as long as the
\mathit{low}
point of every vertex
u
that we meet is lower than
\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we insert
u
into
U_{3}(v)
, provided that it satisfies
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Then, once we reach a vertex with
\mathit{low}
point no lower than
\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we keep traversing this set in reverse order, until we meet one more
u
that satisfies
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, which we also insert into
U_{3}(v)
, and we are done.

Now, if there is a proper ancestor
v^{\prime}
of
v
in
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, then we have that
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
. If
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, then we have that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
is defined. Then we can follow the same process as above in order to compute
U_{3}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, according to Lemma
11.51
, it is sufficient to start from the greatest element of
U_{3}(v)
(i.e., the one that was inserted last into
U_{3}(v)
). In particular, if
U_{3}(v)=\emptyset
, then it is certain that
U_{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, and therefore we are done. Otherwise, we just pick up the computation from the greatest vertex in
U_{3}(v)
. In order to perform efficiently those computations, first we compute, for every vertex
x
, the collection
\mathcal{S}(x)
of the segments of
\widetilde{H}(x)
that are maximal w.r.t. the property that their elements are related as ancestor and descendant. For every vertex
x
, this computation takes
O(|\widetilde{H}(x)|)
time, according to Lemma
6.26
. Since every vertex participates in at most two sets of the form
\widetilde{H}(x)
, we have that the total size of all
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for all vertices
x
, is
O(n)
. Then it is sufficient to process separately all segments of
\mathcal{S}(x)
, for every vertex
x
, as described above, by starting the computation each time from the first vertex
v
of the segment that satisfies
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=x
. The whole procedure is shown in Algorithm
34
. The result is formally stated in Lemma
11.52
.

Lemma 11.53
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices such that
u\in U_{3}(v)
. Then,
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta ii
-
3

4
-cut if and only if:
(1)

w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
(2)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
.

Proof.

(\Rightarrow)
By definition of Type-3
\beta ii
-
3

4
-cuts, we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
. Furthermore, we have
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
, where
e
is the back-edge of the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. This implies that
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
. Lemma
11.49
implies that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a proper ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
v
with
w^{\prime}>w
such that
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Since
M(w^{\prime})=M(w)
and
w^{\prime}>w
, we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
, and Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime})
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
. Furthermore, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then, since
(x,y)\notin B(w)
,
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e\})\sqcup B(w)
implies that
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e\}
. Since
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, we have that
y<w^{\prime}
. Then,
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
implies that
y<\mathit{low}(u)
, in contradiction to
(x,y)\in B(u)
. This shows that
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

(\Leftarrow)
Since
u\in U_{3}(v)
, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, we have that
y\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore
y<v
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
y
, and therefore
v
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
y<v
implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Therefore, since
x
is a descendant of
v
, we have
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}
, this implies that
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}\subseteq B(v)
. Since
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)
. Then we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore
y<w
. Thus,
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
implies that
y<\mathit{low}(u)
. Therefore, we cannot have
(x,y)\in B(u)
. This shows that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
.

Thus, since
B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\}\subseteq B(v)
and
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
and
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
and
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)-1
, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
. Furthermore, since
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(w)
, and therefore
B(v)=(B(u)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\})\sqcup B(w)
implies that
e_{\mathit{high}}(u)\notin B(v)\cup B(w)
. Thus, since
M(w)=M(v)
, we have that
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta ii
-
3

4
-cut.
∎
