11.2.4
Type-3
\beta ii
-
4

4
-cuts

Now we consider case
(4)
of Lemma
11.1
.

Let
u,v,w
be three vertices
\neq r
such that
w
is proper ancestor of
v
,
v
is a proper ancestor of
u
, and there is a back-edge
e\in B(v)
such
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(w)
. By Lemma
11.1
, we have that
C=\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
is a
4
-cut, and we call this a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut.

The following lemma provides some useful information concerning this type of
4
-cuts.

Lemma 11.55
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, and let
e
be the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and either
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, or
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
. If
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
, then
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. This implies that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
.
Since
\mathit{low}(u)
and
w
have
u
as a common descendant, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u)<w
. Then, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
, in contradiction to the fact that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. This shows that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w
.

Now let us assume that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
. (If
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, then there is nothing further to show.) Since
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\geq\mathit{high}(u)
. Thus,
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
implies that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
y>\mathit{high}(u)
. Then,
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. Since
y>\mathit{high}(u)
, the case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected. Furthermore, since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)<y
, the case
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected too. Thus, we have
(x,y)=e
. Therefore, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, we have that
e=\mathit{high}(v)
.

Now let
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
y^{\prime}=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\neq e
. Then we cannot have
y^{\prime}>\mathit{high}(u)
, because otherwise we would conclude as previously that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=e
, which is impossible. Thus, we have
y^{\prime}\leq\mathit{high}(u)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
y^{\prime}<\mathit{high}(u)
. Since
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
, we have that the
\mathit{high}
-edge of
B(u)
is in
B(v)
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x^{\prime\prime},y^{\prime\prime})
in
B(v)
such that
y^{\prime\prime}=\mathit{high}(u)
. Then we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>y^{\prime\prime}>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, which contradicts the definition of the
\mathit{high}_{2}
point. Thus, we conclude that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
.
∎

Lemma 11.56
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex in
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
. Then
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
u
is a descendant of
v
. Thus,
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
implies that
u^{\prime}
is also a descendant of
v
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
, by Lemma
11.55
we have that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
and
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
.

Since
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
, we have that either
\mathit{high}_{1}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, or
\mathit{high}_{2}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. In either case then, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furhermore,
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, by Lemma
11.55
we have that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Then, we have that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=y
. This implies that
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore we have that
(x,y)\notin B(w)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
. Thus, since
(x,y)\in B(v)
and
(x,y)\notin B(w)
, we have that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)=e
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
(x,y)=e
. Since
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
, we have that
y=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
and
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. But then
y=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
contradicts the fact that
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. This shows that
(x,y)\neq e
. Thus, we have that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. This implies that
x
is a common descendant of
u
and
u^{\prime}
. Thus, we have that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then,
u\geq u^{\prime}
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.
∎

Lemma 11.57
.

Let

(*)

Lemma 11.58
.

(u,v,w)

4

. Let

is an ancestor of
u
.

Proof.

Let
e=(x,y)
be the back-edge in the

(u,v,w)
.
Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta

4

. Since
u^{\prime}\in H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
, we have
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. This implies that there is a back-edge
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u^{\prime})
such that
y^{\prime}=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Then,
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, by Lemma
11.55
we have
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus, we have
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=y^{\prime}
. This implies that
y^{\prime}
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore we have
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\notin B(w)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
. Thus, since
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v)
and
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\notin B(w)
, we have that either
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u)
, or
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=e
. The case
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=e
is rejected, because it implies that
y^{\prime}=y
, contradicting the fact that
y^{\prime}=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
y\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus, we have
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(u)
. This implies that
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
u
. Thus,
x^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
u
and
u^{\prime}
, and therefore
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
u\geq u^{\prime}
, this implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
.
∎

Here, we distinguish the following four different cases, depending on the location of the endpoints of the back-edge
e
:

1.

M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
.

2.

M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
.

3.

M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
.

4.

M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
.

The case where
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then, by Lemma
11.55
we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
. Then, we let
V(v)
denote the collection of all vertices
v^{\prime}\neq r
such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
. (We note that
v\in V(v)
.) If a vertex
v\neq r
does not satisfy
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, then we let
V(v)=\emptyset
.

Lemma 11.59
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two distinct vertices such that
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
. Then,
B(v)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}=B(v^{\prime})\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
.

Proof.

Since
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
and
M(v)\neq M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Similarly, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore,
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
is the unique back-edge in
B(v)
whose lower endpoint is
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
is the unique back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
whose lower endpoint is
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
such that
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
v^{\prime}
, and therefore we have that
v
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, we may assume w.l.o.g. that
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\in B(v)
. Then, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)=e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
v
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(v)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(v)\subset B(v^{\prime})
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus B(v)
. Then
y
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. Thus,
x
cannot be a descendant of
v
. Since
M(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
x
, this implies that
M(v^{\prime})
cannot be a descendant of
v
. Let
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. Then,
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
B(v)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
implies that
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
x^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
v
and
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
v
and
M(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
M(v^{\prime})
is not a descendant of
v
, this implies that
M(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v
. Let
c
be the child of
M(v^{\prime})
that is an ancestor of
v
. Since
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\in B(v)
, we have that the higher endpoint of
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
c
.
Now let
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
. If
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
, then we have that
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
c
. If
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
, then we have
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
c
. Thus, in either case we have that
x^{\prime}
is a descendant of
c
. Due to the generality of
(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in B(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
M(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
c
. But this is absurd, since
c
is a child of
M(v^{\prime})
. This shows that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(v)
.

Notice that we cannot have
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\in B(v^{\prime})
. (Because otherwise, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we would have
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)=e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
, contradicting the fact that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(v)
.) Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
, this implies that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. And since
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(v)
, this can be strengthened to
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
, this implies that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(v)
. And since
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\notin B(v^{\prime})
, this can be strengthened to
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. Thus, we have shown that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}=B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Since
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\notin B(v^{\prime})
and
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(v)
, this implies that
B(v)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}=B(v^{\prime})\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
.
∎

Lemma 11.60
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two distinct vertices such that
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
. Then,
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to the same segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant.

Proof.

Since
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
, we have that
M(v)\neq M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, both
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
. Furthermore, we have that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
is a common descendant of
M(v)
and
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a common descendant of
v
and
v^{\prime}
. Thus,
v
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. We may assume w.l.o.g. that
v
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. This implies that
v>v^{\prime}
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
v
and
v^{\prime}
do not belong to a segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
with the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
\widetilde{H}
is sorted in decreasing order, this means that there is a vertex
v^{\prime\prime}\in\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
such that
v>v^{\prime\prime}>v^{\prime}
, and
v^{\prime\prime}
is not an ancestor of
v
. Notice that, since
v>v^{\prime\prime}>v^{\prime}
and
v
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
v^{\prime\prime}
is also a descendant of
v^{\prime}
.

Since
v^{\prime\prime}\in\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
we have that either
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, or
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Thus, in either case, there is a back-edge
(x,y)
in
B(v^{\prime\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore, we have
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Notice that we cannot have that
x
is a descendant of
v
(because otherwise,
x
is a common descendant of
v
and
v^{\prime\prime}
, and therefore
v
and
v^{\prime\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant, which is impossible, since
v^{\prime\prime}<v
and
v^{\prime\prime}
is not an ancestor of
v
). This implies that
(x,y)\notin B(v)
. Thus, we have
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus B(v)
. Lemma
11.59
implies that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus B(v)=\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Thus,
(x,y)=e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
. But
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to a segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
with the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant, and so they belong to a maximal such segment.
∎

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
.
We let
\widetilde{W}(v)
denote the collection of all ancestors
w
of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. We also let
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v):=\mathit{max}(\widetilde{W}(v))
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v):=\mathit{min}(\widetilde{W}(v))
. (If
\widetilde{W}(v)=\emptyset
, then we let
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v):=\bot
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v):=\bot
.)

Lemma 11.61
.

The values
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
can be computed in linear time in total, for all vertices
v\neq r
.

Proof.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex. If
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
or
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, then by definition we have
\widetilde{W}(v)=\emptyset
, and therefore
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)=\bot
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)=\bot
. So let us assume that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
.

Let
x=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. Then, notice that
\widetilde{W}(v)
consists of all vertices
w
with
M(w)=x
that are ancestors of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Let
w=\mathit{lastM}(x)
. If
w>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, then we have
\widetilde{W}(v)=\emptyset
, because this implies that every vertex
w^{\prime}
with
M(w^{\prime})=x
has
w^{\prime}>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore it cannot be an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Now suppose that
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. We have that
x
is a common descendant of
w
and
v
, and therefore
w
and
v
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
implies that
w<v
, and therefore
w
is an ancestor of
v
. Then, since
v
is a common descendant of
w
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
w
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Thus, we have
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, and since
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)=\mathit{min}(\widetilde{W}(v))
, we have
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)=w
. Thus,
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
can be easily computed in constant time, for every vertex
v
.

If we have established that
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)\neq\bot
, then, in order to compute
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
, we use Algorithm
12
. Specifically, we generate a query of the form
q(M^{-1}(x),\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
. This is to return the greatest
w
with
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
such that
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then we can show as previously that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore we have that
w
is the greatest ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. Thus, we have
w=\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
. Since the number of all those queries is
O(n)
, Lemma
8.5
implies that Algorithm
12
can compute all of them in
O(n)
time in total.
∎

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
.
Let
\widetilde{S}
be the segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant (i.e.,
\widetilde{S}=\widetilde{S}_{2}(v)
). Then,
U_{4}^{1}(v)
is the collection of all vertices
u\in\widetilde{S}
such that:
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
(2)

\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
, and
(3)
either
\mathit{low}(u)<\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}(v)}
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}
that satisfies
(1)
,
(2)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
.

Lemma 11.62
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
. Let us assume that
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to the same segment
\widetilde{S}
of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us further assume that
v^{\prime}\notin V(v)
,
\widetilde{W}(v)\neq\emptyset
and
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. If
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{4}^{1}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{4}^{1}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

First we will show that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, and
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
,
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
, and
v^{\prime}\notin V(v)
, we have
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
(because this is the only condition that prevents
v^{\prime}
from being in
V(v)
).

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
is the unique back-edge in
B(v)
whose lower endpoint is
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Similarly, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})
is the unique back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
whose lower endpoint is
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
.

Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, we have that
(x,y)\neq e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. Thus, we have that
x
is a common descendant of
v^{\prime}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. This shows that
v^{\prime}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
are related as ancestor and descendant.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
is not a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Then we have that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
, this implies that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Notice that, if
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\in B(v)
, then, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
. Thus, whether
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\in B(v)
or
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(v)
, we infer that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
can be strengthened to
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Then
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
, this implies that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(v)
. As previously, we can argue that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(v)
can be strengthened to
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}\subseteq B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. Thus, we have shown that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}=B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
, and therefore we have
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
, a contradiction. This shows that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
.

Now let
w
be a vertex in
\widetilde{W}(v)
, and let
w^{\prime}
be a vertex in
\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
. Then we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
w
and
w^{\prime}
have a common descendant, and therefore they are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}
is not a proper ancestor of
w
. Then we have that
w^{\prime}
is a descendant of
w
. Since
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, we have that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. And since
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
M(w^{\prime})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
. Since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, and
v^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
, we have that
M(w)
is a proper ancestor of
M(w^{\prime})
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)
such that
x
is not a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
(since
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
implies that
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
). Furthermore, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. But this implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
, a contradiction. This shows that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Due to the generality of
w^{\prime}\in\widetilde{W}(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(w^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
w
. And due to the generality of
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, this implies that
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
, and
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
. Since
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}
, we have that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
(since
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
implies that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
). This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
.

We have that
M(\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime}))=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
and
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
M(\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime}))
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, since
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Thus, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime}))\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})<\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
, we have
y<\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
y<\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
(since
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})<\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
). Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)<\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
. But this contradicts the fact that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
(which is an implication of
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
). This shows that
u
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u\neq v^{\prime}
. Thus,
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Thus, we have the following facts:
u\in\widetilde{S}
,
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
,
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)>\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
. But this implies that
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
(because we can consider the lowest
u
that has those properties). A contradiction. This shows that if
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{4}^{1}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{4}^{1}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
that is lower than the greatest vertex
u^{\prime}
in
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
.
Since
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
we have that
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}
. This implies that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Thus, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y<\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
.

Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
u^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
. Therefore, since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is the lowest proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{S}
such that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})

(*)
.

Now we will trace the implications of
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
. First, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Then, we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)>\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
(since
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
). Finally, we can show as above that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the proof of this fact above did not rely on
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
). But then, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have a contradiction to
(*)
.
Thus, we have shown that every vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
. In particular, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{1}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Algorithm 36

Compute all sets
U_{4}^{1}(v)
, for a collection of vertices
\mathcal{V}
that satisfies the properties described in Lemma
11.63

Lemma 11.63
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a collection of vertices such that:

(1)

For every
v\in\mathcal{V}
, we have
v\neq r
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
.

(2)

For every
v,v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}
with
v\neq v^{\prime}
, we have
v^{\prime}\notin V(v)
.

(3)

For every
v\in\mathcal{V}
, we have
\widetilde{W}(v)\neq\emptyset
, and the vertices
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)
are computed.

Then, Algorithm
36
correctly computes the sets
U_{4}^{1}(v)
, for all vertices
v\in\mathcal{V}
. Furthermore, on input
\mathcal{V}
, Algorithm
36
runs in linear time.

Proof.

The proof is the same as that of Lemma
11.39
(which is given in the main text, in the two paragraphs right above Algorithm
30
). Notice that the difference between Algorithm
30
and Algorithm
36
is that the second algorithm has a different set
\mathcal{V}
of vertices for which the
U_{4}^{1}
sets are defined, and the occurrences of “
\mathit{firstW}
” and “
\mathit{lastW}
” are replaced with “
\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}
” and “
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}
”, respectively. Now we can use the argument of Lemma
11.39
, by just replacing the references to Lemma
11.38
with references to Lemma
11.62
.
∎

Lemma 11.64
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then
u\in U_{4}^{1}(v)
. Furthermore, for every
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
we have that
(u,v^{\prime},w)
is a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, by Lemma
11.55
we have that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Now let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex with
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
such that
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}(u)
, Lemma
11.56
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. Thus, we have that
u
and
v
belong to the same segment
\widetilde{S}
of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
. By Lemma
11.55
we have that
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
and
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Since
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. This shows that
w\in\widetilde{W}(v)
, and therefore
w\leq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
. Since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
and
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)\leq w
, we have
\widetilde{\mathit{lastW}}(v)\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Now, if
\mathit{low}(u)<\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
, then
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{1}(v)
. Otherwise, let us assume that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
. Then, there is a vertex
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
u^{\prime}<u
,
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
. Since both
u
and
u^{\prime}
are in
\widetilde{S}
, we have that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
u^{\prime}<u
implies that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore, since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
. This implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. Since
y\geq\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)\geq w
, we have that
(x,y)
cannot be in
B(w)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Thus, since
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
, we have that
e\notin B(u^{\prime})
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(u)
is the only viable option. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, this implies that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Thus, we have
B(u^{\prime})=B(u)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. This shows that
u
is the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{firstW}}(v)
. Thus,
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{1}(v)
.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, we have that
v\in V(v)
. Now let
v^{\prime}
be a vertex in
V(v)
such that
v^{\prime}\neq v
. Then, by Lemma
11.59
we have
B(v)\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}=B(v^{\prime})\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. This implies that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}=B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Also,
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
implies that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}=B(u)\sqcup B(w)
. Thus, we infer that
B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}=B(u)\sqcup B(w)
, and therefore
B(v^{\prime})=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\cup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
.

Since
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. This implies that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}(u)
(since
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(u)
). Thus, we cannot have
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\in B(u)
. Furthermore, since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\notin B(w)
. Thus,
B(v^{\prime})=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\cup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
can be strengthened to
B(v^{\prime})=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\}
. Finally, since
v^{\prime}\in V(v)
, we have that
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v^{\prime})\})=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(w)
. Thus, we conclude that
(u,v^{\prime},w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut.
∎

Lemma 11.65
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices such that

Lemma 11.67
.

For all vertices
v\neq r
, the values
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)

Proof.

First, we need to have the values

computed, for all vertices

6.20
, this can be achieved in linear time in total. Now, in order to compute

. By Lemma

time in total.

6.3
implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
.
Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have that
|B(v^{\prime})|>1
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
. Then, since
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
, we have that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(x,y)\neq e_{L}(v)
, this can be strengthened to
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
. This implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
. Thus, we have that
x
is a common descendant of
v^{\prime}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
, and therefore
v^{\prime}
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
are related as ancestor and descendant.

If
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, then we have that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
is a proper ancestor of
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
, since
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
is a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. So let us assume that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
, this shows that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}\subseteq B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
and
B(v)\neq B(v^{\prime})
(since the graph is
3
-edge-connected), we have that
B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}=B(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})=M(v^{\prime})
. Since
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})\neq M(v^{\prime})
, we have that
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
is a proper descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
. Therefore, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})=M(v^{\prime})
, we have that
M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
is a proper descendant of
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
.

Now let
w
be a vertex in
W_{L}(v)
, and let
w^{\prime}
be a vertex in
W_{L}(v^{\prime})
. Then we have that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
and
M(w^{\prime})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
. Thus, we have that
M(w^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(w)
, and therefore a proper descendant of
w
. Thus, since
M(w^{\prime})
is a common descendant of
w^{\prime}
and
w
, we have that
w^{\prime}
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}
is not a proper ancestor of
w
. Then,
w^{\prime}
is a descendant of
w
. Since
M(w^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
M(w)
, there is a back-edge
(x,y)
in
B(w)
such that
x
is not a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
, a contradiction. Thus, we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Due to the generality of
w^{\prime}\in W_{L}(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
w
. And due to the generality of
w\in W_{L}(v)
, this implies that
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
, and
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
. Since
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
, we have that
u\in S
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}\in S
, we have that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Since
W_{L}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
, we let
w^{\prime}=\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(w^{\prime})
. Then,
x
is a descendant
M(w^{\prime})=M(B(v^{\prime})\setminus\{e_{L}(v^{\prime})\})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Thus, since
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, this shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Therefore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
(since
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
implies that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
). Thus, since
x
is a descendant of
u
, this shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Since
y=\mathit{low}(w^{\prime})
and
w^{\prime}=\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
y<\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
y<\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
(since
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
). Since
(x,y)\in B(u)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
. But this contradicts the fact that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
(which is an implication of
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
). Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Thus, we have the following facts:
u\in S
,
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)>\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
. But this implies that
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
(because we can consider the lowest
u
that has those properties). A contradiction. This shows that if
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{4}^{2}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{4}^{2}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
that is lower than the greatest vertex
u^{\prime}
in
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
.
Since
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
, we have that
u\in S
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
we have that
u^{\prime}\in S
. This implies that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Thus, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y<\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
.

Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper descendant of
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
u^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is the lowest vertex in
S
that is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
such that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})

(*)
.

Now we will trace the implications of
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
. First, we have that
u\in S
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)>\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
(since
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
). Finally, we can show as above that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the proof of this fact above did not rely on
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
). But then, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have a contradiction to
(*)
.
Thus, we have shown that every vertex in
U_{4}^{2}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
. In particular, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{2}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{2}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Lemma 11.69
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be the collection of all vertices
v\neq r
such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
W_{L}(v)\neq\emptyset
, and suppose that the vertices
\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
and
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
are computed for every
v\in\mathcal{V}
. Then, Algorithm
38
correctly computes the sets
U_{4}^{2}(v)
, for all vertices
v\in\mathcal{V}
, in total linear time.

Proof.

The proof is the same as that of Lemma
11.39
(which is given in the main text, in the two paragraphs right above Algorithm
30
). Notice that the difference between Algorithm
30
and Algorithm
38
is that the second algorithm has a different set
\mathcal{V}
of vertices for which the
U_{4}^{2}
sets are defined, and the occurrences of “
\mathit{firstW}
” and “
\mathit{lastW}
” are replaced with “
\mathit{firstW_{L}}
” and “
\mathit{lastW_{L}}
”, respectively. Now we can use the argument of Lemma
11.39
, by just replacing the references to Lemma
11.38
with references to Lemma
11.68
.
∎

Lemma 11.70
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, and let
u
be a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
. Then,
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u)
.

Proof.

Since
u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. This implies that
M(u)
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Thus, since
M(u)
is a common descendant of
u
and
M(v)
, we have that
u
and
M(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
M(v)
. Thus, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
M(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
, this implies that
B(v)\subseteq B(u)
. Thus,
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
implies that
B(u)=B(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. This shows that
u
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is an ancestor of
L_{1}(v)
(i.e., the higher endpoint of
e_{L}(v)
). Then, since
u
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
, we cannot have
M(v)=L_{1}(v)
. Thus,
L_{1}(v)
is a proper descendant of
M(v)
. So let
c
be the child of
M(v)
that is an ancestor of
L_{1}(v)
. Then, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, we have that
e_{L}(v)
is the unique back-edge in
B(v)
whose higher endpoint is a descendant of
c
. Now, since
u
is an ancestor of
L_{1}(v)
and a proper descendant of
M(v)
, we have that
u
is also a descendant of
c
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, we have that
|B(u)|>1
. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(u)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(x,y)\neq e_{L}(v)
, this can be strengthened to
(x,y)\in B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
. Thus, we have that in
B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\}
there is still a back-edge whose higher endpoint is a descendant of
c
(i.e.,
(x,y)
), which is impossible. We conclude that
u
is not an ancestor of
L_{1}(v)
, and therefore
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u)
.
∎

Lemma 11.71
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
, such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
. Then
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a
4
-cut, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex such that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
and
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(u)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, this implies that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore
u^{\prime}\in H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
. Then, since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, by Lemma
11.57
we have that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. This shows that
u
and
v
belong to a segment
S
of
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant.

Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
, we have that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
. Thus, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, we have that
w\in W_{L}(v)
, and therefore
w\geq\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
. By Lemma
11.55
, we have that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and therefore
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus, if
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
, then
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{2}(v)
. So let us assume that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not the lowest vertex in
S
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
. Then, there is a vertex
u^{\prime}
in
S
that is lower than
u
, it is a proper descendant of
v
, and has
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
. Since both
u
and
u^{\prime}
are in
S
, they are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u^{\prime}
is lower than
u
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
u
. Since both
u
and
u^{\prime}
are in
S
, we have that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
. Thus, Lemma
6.3
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
, and therefore an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(v)
(because
u^{\prime}\in S
, and therefore
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
), and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e_{L}(v)\}
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(v)
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e_{L}(v)
. Since
y\geq\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)\geq w
, we have that
y
cannot be a proper ancestor of
w
, and so the case
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected. Then, since
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(v)
, Lemma
11.70
implies that
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u^{\prime})
. Therefore
(x,y)\neq e_{L}(v)
. Thus, since
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected, the only viable option is
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, this implies that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Thus, since
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
, we have that
B(u^{\prime})=B(u)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, we have that
u
is the lowest vertex in
S
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{firstW_{L}}(v)
. This means that
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{2}(v)
.
∎

Lemma 11.72
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices such that
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u)
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
. Then,
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
if and only if:
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, and
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Proof.

(
\Rightarrow
) Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a proper ancestor

Since

. This can be strengthened to

, since the graph is

. Then,

, and therefore a descendant of

. Furthermore,

, and therefore a proper ancestor of

. This shows that

, or

). Thus, we have that

.

(
\Leftarrow
) We have to show that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e_{L}(v)\}
, and

, which is impossible).

Let

. This shows that

. Due to the generality of

.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in

. Then,

, and therefore a descendant of

, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of

.

Since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
, we have that the higher endpoint of

. Since

, this implies that

. By assumption, we have

. Therefore, we have
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u)\cup B(w)
.

Thus, we have

,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
, and
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. This implies that

. Therefore, since
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, we have that there is a back-edge

, such that

. Since

, this implies that

. By assumption, we have

.

Proposition 11.73
.

Algorithm
39
correctly computes all Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cuts of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(v)\}
, where
u
is a descendant of
v
,
v
is a descendant of
w
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

Proof.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut with back-edge
e_{L}(v)
such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and

. By the definition of Type-3
\beta

4

4
-cuts, this implies that

. Then, by Lemma

we have that

. Then, by Lemma

we have that
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of

with

such that

. This implies that

. Thus, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
and

, we have that
v
is in the collection
\mathcal{V}
, computed in Line
39
. Then, notice that
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(v)\}
(i.e., the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
) will be correctly marked by Algorithm
39
in Line
39
.

Conversely, suppose that a
4
-element set
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(v)\}
is marked by Algorithm
39
in Line
39
. Then we have that:
(1)

v
is a vertex such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})\neq M(v)
(due to
v\in\mathcal{V}
),
(2)

u\in U_{4}^{2}(v)
,
(3)

w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and
(4)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
and
e_{L}(v)\notin B(u)
. Thus, Lemma
11.72
implies that
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e_{L}(v)\}
is a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut. Since

, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
.

Now we will show that Algorithm
39
has a linear-time implementation. First, by Proposition
6.20
, we can compute
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
for all vertices
v\neq r
, in total linear time. By Lemma
11.67
, we have that the values

and
\mathit{lastW_{L}}(v)
can be computed in linear time in total, for all vertices
v\neq r
. Then, we can check in constant time whether

, for a vertex
v\neq r
, by simply checking whether e.g.

. Thus, the set
\mathcal{V}
in Line

can be computed in linear time. By Lemma
11.69
, we have that the sets

can be computed in total linear time, for all vertices

, using Algorithm
38
. Thus, the
for
loop in Line
39
can be performed in linear time. In particular, we have that the total size of all
U_{4}^{2}
sets is
O(n)
.

It remains to show how to find the vertex
w
in Line
39
. To do this, we use Algorithm
12
. Specifically, let
v
be a vertex in
\mathcal{V}
, let
u
be a vertex in
U_{4}^{2}(v)
, and let
x=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
. Then we generate a query
q(M^{-1}(x),\mathit{min}\{\mathit{low}(u),p(v)\})
. This is to return the greatest vertex
w
such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
and
w\leq p(v)
. Since
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
, we have that
M(w)
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Thus,
M(w)
is a common descendant of
v
and
w
, and therefore
v
and
w
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,

implies that
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and so
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{L}(v)\})
and

. Now, using Algorithm
12
we can answer all those queries in total linear time, according to Lemma
8.5
. Thus, the

loop in Line
39
can be performed in linear time. We conclude that Algorithm
39
runs in linear time.

The case where
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Then, by Lemma
11.55
we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, and
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
. Furthermore, by Lemma
11.55
we have that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)<\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus, since
\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)<\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, we have
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)<\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Since
M(w)=M(v)
, this implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
.

Now let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. We let
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
denote the greatest proper ancestor
w
of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
such that
M(w)=M(v)
.

Lemma 11.74
.

Let
v\neq r
be a vertex such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
is either
\mathit{nextM}(v)
or
\mathit{nextM}(\mathit{nextM}(v))
.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)<\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
are both ancestors of
v
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Since
\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
v
have the same
M
point, we have that
\mathit{lastM}(v)
is related as ancestor and descendant with
v
. Due to the minimality of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
in
M^{-1}(M(v))
, this implies that
\mathit{lastM}(v)
is an ancestor of
v
. Thus, since
v
is a common descendant of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
implies that
\mathit{lastM}(v)
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Therefore,
\mathit{lastM}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. This shows that
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\neq\bot
.

Now suppose that
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\neq\mathit{nextM}(v)
. By Lemma
6.6
we have that
\mathit{nextM}(v)
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus,
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\neq\mathit{nextM}(v)
implies that
\mathit{nextM}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. By definition,
\mathit{nextM}(\mathit{nextM}(v))
is the greatest proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v)
that has the same
M
point with
v
. Thus, since
\mathit{nextM}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{nextM}(\mathit{nextM}(v))
is the greatest proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
that has the same
M
point as
v
. In other words,
\mathit{nextM}(\mathit{nextM}(v))=\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
.
∎

Now let
S
be the segment of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that contains
v
and is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant (i.e., we have
S=\widetilde{S}_{2}(v)
). Then, we let
U_{4}^{3}(v)
denote the collection of all vertices
u\in S
such that:
(1)

u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
(2)

\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and
(3)
either
\mathit{low}(u)<\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
, or
u
is the lowest vertex in
S
that satisfies
(1)
,
(2)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
.

Lemma 11.75
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Let
w
and
w^{\prime}
be two vertices such that
M(w)=M(v)
,
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
, and both
w
and
w^{\prime}
are ancestors of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Then

is a proper ancestor of

.

Proof.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that

. Then
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,

is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that

, and therefore
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
. Thus, since
x
is a common descendant of
M(v)
and
v^{\prime}
, we have that
M(v)
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
M(v)
is not a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Then we have that
M(v)
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. We have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
and
v
are related as ancestor and descendant, since both have
v^{\prime}
as a common descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
v
. Then we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
v
. Now consider a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(v)
such that
y=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
is a descendant of
v
, we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
is a proper descendant of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})>\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Since
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\geq\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Since
\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, this implies that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)\geq\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. But this contradicts
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. This shows that our last supposition cannot be true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
v
.

Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
, this implies that
B(v)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus we have
B(v^{\prime})=B(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. This shows that
M(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
.

Now let
w
and
w^{\prime}
be two vertices such that
M(w)=M(v)
,
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
, and both
w
and
w^{\prime}
are ancestors of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Then
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}
is not a proper ancestor of
w
. Then we have that
w^{\prime}
is a descendant of
w
. Since
M(v)=M(w)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w)
such that
x
is not a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(w)=M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendnant of
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. But we have that
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
x
must be a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. This contradicts the fact that
x
is not a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Thus, we have that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
w
.

Lemma 11.76
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})\neq\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
,
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
\mathit{lastM}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
,
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
, and both
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to the same segment
\widetilde{S}
of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant (i.e., we have
\widetilde{S}=\widetilde{S}(v)=\widetilde{S}(v^{\prime})
). If
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{4}^{3}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{4}^{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

Notice that, since
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v^{\prime})\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
, we have that both
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
and
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
are well-defined. Furthermore, Lemma
11.75
implies that
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
and
U_{4}^{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be a vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}
, we have that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
. Lemma
6.4
implies that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now, since
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. But then we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then, since
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
is not empty (because we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{S}(v^{\prime})=\widetilde{S}(v)
such that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
). This contradicts our supposition that
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Thus, we have shown that
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
implies that
U_{4}^{3}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{4}^{3}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
is not empty. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
that is lower than the greatest vertex
u^{\prime}
in
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
.
Since
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
we have that
u^{\prime}\in\widetilde{S}
. This implies that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Thus, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
.

Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper descendant of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
u^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Therefore, since
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is the lowest proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{S}
with
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})

(*)
.

Now we will trace the implications of
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
. First, we have that
u\in\widetilde{S}
. Then, we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)>\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
(since
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
). Finally, we can show as above that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the proof of this fact above did not rely on
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
). But then, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have a contradiction to
(*)
.
Thus, we have shown that every vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
. In particular, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{3}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Algorithm 40

Compute the sets

, for all vertices

such that

and
