Lemma 11.77
.

Algorithm
40
correctly computes the sets
U_{4}^{3}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Furthermore, it runs in linear time.

Proof.

The proof here is similar as that of Lemma
11.52
(which was given in the main text, in the two paragraphs above Algorithm
34
). The differences are the following. First, the set
\mathcal{V}
of the vertices for which the sets
U_{4}^{3}
are defined is given by all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\neq\bot
. Due to Lemma
11.74
, it is easy to collect all those vertices in
O(n)
time. I.e., we have to check, for every vertex
v\neq r
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, whether
\mathit{nextM}(v)
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. If that is the case, then
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)=\mathit{nextM}(v)
. Otherwise,
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)=\mathit{nextM}(\mathit{nextM}(v))
(which may be
\mathit{null}
). Second, here we process the vertices
v
in their
\widetilde{S}_{2}(v)
segment (instead of the
\widetilde{S}_{1}(v)
). Thus, in Lines
40
and
40
, we check whether
v
satisfies
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=x
(where
x
is the vertex for which we process the
\widetilde{H}(x)
list). And third, we have that every
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
satisfies
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Thus, in Lines
40
and
40
we have the appropriate condition (where is it checked whether
\mathit{high}_{1}(u)=x
). Then the proof follows the same reasoning as in Lemma
11.52
. The main difference in the argument here is that every reference to Lemma
11.51
is replaced with a reference to Lemma
11.76
.
∎

Lemma 11.78
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
. Then
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, Lemma
11.55
implies that
\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
. Thus, we may consider the segment
\widetilde{S}
of
\widetilde{H}(\mathit{high}_{2}(v))
from
u
to
v
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex in
\widetilde{S}
. Then, we have that
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
, and therefore Lemma
11.56
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. Thus, we have that all elements of
\widetilde{S}
are related as ancestor and descendant (since all of them are ancestors of
u
).
Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, Lemma
11.55
implies that
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Furthermore, Lemma
11.55
implies that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus, since
\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, we have that
w\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Then, since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
, and therefore
\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
is defined (and it is greater than, or equal to,
w
). Also, we have
w\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Thus, if
\mathit{low}(u)<\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
, then
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
. So let us assume that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
. Then, there is a vertex
u^{\prime}
in
\widetilde{S}
, that is a proper ancestor of
u
and a proper descendant of
v
, such that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
.
Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this shows that
B(u)\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
. Then we have that
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore it is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then,
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. The case
(x,y)\in B(w)
is rejected, since
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)\geq w
. Furthermore, since
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
and
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})
, we cannot have
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\in B(u^{\prime})
, and therefore the case
(x,y)=e
is also rejected.
Thus, we have that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u^{\prime})
, this shows that
B(u^{\prime})\subseteq B(u)
. Thus, we have
B(u)=B(u^{\prime})
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, we have shown that
u
is the lowest vertex in
\widetilde{S}
that is a proper descendant of
v
such that
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
,
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
and
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\widetilde{\mathit{nextM}}(v)
. We conclude that
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{3}(v)
.
∎

Lemma 11.79
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
and
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
. Then,
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut if and only if:
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, and
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Proof.

(
\Rightarrow
) Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Thus, we get
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, by Lemma
11.55
we have
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
. Furthermore, Lemma
11.55
implies that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
. Thus, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
, we have
M(w)=M(v)
.

Now let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a proper ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
v
with
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, such that
w^{\prime}>w
. Then, since
M(v)=M(w)
and
M(v)=M(w^{\prime})
, we have that
M(v)
is a common descendant of
w
and
w^{\prime}
, and therefore
w
and
w^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus,
w^{\prime}>w
implies that
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
.
Since
w^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
w
with
M(w^{\prime})=M(w)
, Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
. This can be strengthened to
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime})
, since the graph is
3
-edge-connected. Thus, there is a back-edge
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})\setminus B(w)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
, this implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. The case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected, since
y<w^{\prime}
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and therefore
y<\mathit{low}(u)
. The case
(x,y)=e
is also rejected, because
e=e_{\mathit{high}}(v)
, and
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)\geq\mathit{low}(u)\geq w^{\prime}
. Thus, we have that
(x,y)\in B(w)
, a contradiction. This shows that
w
is the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

(
\Leftarrow
) We have to show that there is a back-edge
e
such that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
, and
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
.

Since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
and
M(w)=M(v)
, we have that
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
. Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)>\mathit{high}(u)
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\notin B(u)
. And since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)\leq\mathit{high}(u)<\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, we have that
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\notin B(w)
. Furthermore, since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, we have that
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
(because, if there existed a back-edge in
B(u)\cap B(w)
, its lower endpoint would be lower than
\mathit{low}(u)
, which is impossible). This shows that the sets
B(u)
,
B(w)
and
\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
are pairwise disjoint.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Since
u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)
, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
. Thus,
(x,y)\in B(u)
implies that
x
is a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, we have that
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(w)=M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w)
, this implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
.

Thus, we have
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
,
B(w)\subseteq B(v)
,
e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\in B(v)
, and the sets
B(u)
,
B(w)
and
\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
are pairwise disjoint. Thus,
(B(u)\sqcup B(v))\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}\subseteq B(v)
. Since
\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, this implies that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\}
. By assumption we have
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
. Therefore, since
M(w)=M(v)
, we have
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})
.
∎

let
\mathcal{V}
be the collection of all vertices
v\neq r
such that
M(B(v)\setminus\{e_{\mathit{high}}(v)\})=M(v)
,
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)\neq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)
and
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{high}_{2}(v)

1

foreach

v\in\mathcal{V}

do

2

compute
U_{4}^{3}(v)

3

end foreach

4

foreach

v\in\mathcal{V}

do

5

foreach

u\in U_{4}^{3}(v)

do

6

let
w
be the greatest proper ancestor of
v
with
M(w)=M(v)
such that
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)

Proof.

Now we will show that Algorithm

Lemma 11.81
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
with
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Then,
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
.

Proof.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that and
y=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Then, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, we have that
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Thus, we have that
M(v)
is an ancestor of
x
. Therefore, since
x
is a common descendant of
v^{\prime}
and
M(v)
, we have that
v^{\prime}
and
M(v)
are related as ancestor and descendant.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
M(v)
is not a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Then, we have that
M(v)
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, this implies that
B(v^{\prime})\subseteq B(v)
. Conversely, let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v)
. Then,
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(v)
, this implies that
B(v)\subseteq B(v^{\prime})
. Thus we have
B(v^{\prime})=B(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that the graph is
3
-edge-connected. This shows that
M(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
.

Let
w
and
w^{\prime}
be two vertices such that
M(w)=M(v)
,
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
,
w\leq\mathit{nextM}(v)
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Then, Lemma
6.6
implies that
w
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
and
w^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
w
and
w^{\prime}
have a common descendant, and therefore they are related as ancestor and descendant.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w^{\prime}
is not a proper ancestor of
w
. Then, we have that
w^{\prime}
is a descendant of
w
. Since
M(w)=M(v)
is a proper ancestor of
v^{\prime}
, there is a back-edge
(x,y)
in
B(w)
such that
x
is not a descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Therefore,
x
is not a descendant of
M(v^{\prime})=M(w^{\prime})
. Since
x
is a descendant of
M(v)
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
w^{\prime}
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
. But this implies that
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})=M(v^{\prime})
, a contradiction.
This shows that
w^{\prime}
is a proper ancestor of
w
. Due to the generality of
w^{\prime}
and
w
, this implies that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
.
∎

Lemma 11.82
.

Let
v
and
v^{\prime}
be two vertices
\neq r
with
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})\neq\bot
, such that
v^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v
,
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
, and both
v
and
v^{\prime}
belong to the same segment
S
of
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
that is maximal w.r.t. the property that all its elements are related as ancestor and descendant (i.e., we have
S=S(v)=S(v^{\prime})
). If
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
, then
U_{4}^{4}(v)=\emptyset
. If
U_{4}^{4}(v)\neq\emptyset
, then the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
.

Proof.

By Lemma
11.81
, we have that
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
and
U_{4}^{4}(v)\neq\emptyset
. Let
u
be a vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Since
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
, we have that
u\in S
. Thus, since
v^{\prime}\in S
, we have that
u
and
v^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Since
u
is not a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is an ancestor of
v^{\prime}
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(v^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
. Lemma
6.4
implies that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now, since
(x,y)\in B(v^{\prime})
, we have that
x
is a descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. But then we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y=\mathit{low}(v^{\prime})<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
. Then, since
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
, we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. This implies that
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
is not empty (because we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v^{\prime}
in
S(v^{\prime})=S(v)
such that
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
). This contradicts our supposition that
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})\neq\emptyset
. Thus, we have shown that
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
implies that
U_{4}^{4}(v)=\emptyset
.

Now let us assume that
U_{4}^{4}(v)\neq\emptyset
. This implies that
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
is not empty. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there is a vertex
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
that is lower than the greatest vertex
u^{\prime}
in
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
.
Since
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
, we have
u\in S
. Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
we have
u^{\prime}\in S
. This implies that
u
and
u^{\prime}
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have that
u
is a proper ancestor of
u^{\prime}
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Then, since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
. Now let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u^{\prime})
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u^{\prime}
, and therefore a descendant of
u
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
u
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(u)
. Thus, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\leq y<\mathit{lastM}(v)
, in contradiction to the fact that
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Thus, our last supposition is not true, and therefore we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
.

Since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
, and therefore a proper descendant of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Thus,
u^{\prime}
is a common descendant of
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
and
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
are related as ancestor and descendant. Thus, since
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is not a proper ancestor of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})
is a descendant of
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
. Thus, since
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
, we have that
u^{\prime}
is the lowest proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
in
S
with
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
such that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})

(*)
.

Now we will trace the implications of
u\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
. First, we have
u\in S
. Then, we have
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}_{1}(v^{\prime})
. Furthermore, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{lastM}(v)
, and therefore
\mathit{low}(u)>\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
(since
\mathit{nextM}(v^{\prime})
is a proper ancestor of
\mathit{lastM}(v)
). Finally, we can show as above that
u
is a proper descendant of
v^{\prime}
(the proof of this fact above did not rely on
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})=\emptyset
). But then, since
u
is lower than
u^{\prime}
, we have a contradiction to
(*)
.
Thus, we have shown that every vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
is at least as great as the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
. In particular, this implies that the lowest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
is greater than, or equal to, the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v^{\prime})
.
∎

Lemma 11.83
.

Algorithm
42
correctly computes the sets
U_{4}^{4}(v)
, for all vertices
v\neq r
such that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
. Furthermore, it has a linear-time implementation.

Proof.

The argument is almost identical to that provided for Lemma
11.25
in the main text (in the three paragraphs above Algorithm

). The only difference is that here we care about the
\mathit{low}
point of the vertices
u
(and not for their
\mathit{low}_{2}
point). This does not affect the analysis of correctness, because the computation is performed in segments of

Lemma 11.84
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices that induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, such that
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
and
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
, where
e
is the back-edge in the
4
-cut induced by
(u,v,w)
. Suppose that the lower endpoint of
e
is distinct from
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Then
U_{4}^{4}(v)\neq\emptyset
, and let
\tilde{u}
be the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
. If
u\notin U_{4}^{4}(v)
, then
u
is the predecessor of
\tilde{u}
in
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
.

Proof.

Since
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
and
u
is a proper descendant of
v
, we may consider the segment
S
of
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
from
u
to
v
. Let
u^{\prime}
be a vertex in
S
. Due to the sorting of
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
, we have
u\geq u^{\prime}\geq v
. Thus, since the lower endpoint of
e
is distinct from
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, Lemma
11.58
implies that
u^{\prime}
is an ancestor of
u
. Thus, we have that all elements of
S
are related as ancestor and descendant (since all of them are ancestors of
u
), and therefore
S\subseteq S(v)
.
Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have
M(w)=M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})
. Therefore, since
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
, we have
M(w)=M(v)
. Since
w
is a proper ancestor of
v
, this implies that
\mathit{nextM}(v)\neq\bot
, and
w\leq\mathit{nextM}(v)
.

By Lemma
11.55
we have
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, and therefore
\mathit{lastM}(v)\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. Thus, if
\mathit{low}(u)<\mathit{nextM}(v)
, then
u
satisfies enough conditions to be in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Otherwise, we have
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, and therefore
U_{4}^{4}(v)
is not empty, because we can consider the lowest proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v
in
S(v)
such that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
. So let
\tilde{u}
be the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u\notin U_{4}^{4}(v)
, and
u
is not the predecessor of
\tilde{u}
in
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
.

Since
u
is a proper descendant of
v
in
S(v)
such that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
, we have that there is a proper descendant
u^{\prime}
of
v
in
S(v)
that is lower than
u
and has
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\geq\mathit{nextM}(v)
(because this is the only condition that prevents
u
from being in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
). Thus, we may consider the lowest vertex
u^{\prime}
that has this property. Then, we have that
u^{\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
, and every other vertex
u^{\prime\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
satisfies
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v)
. Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
u^{\prime}
is not the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
. Then there is a vertex
u^{\prime\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
such that
u^{\prime\prime}>u^{\prime}
. Since

and
u^{\prime\prime}\in U_{4}^{4}(v)
, we have

and

. Therefore,

is a proper descendant of
u^{\prime}
. Furthermore, we have
\mathit{high}(u^{\prime})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u^{\prime\prime})
. Thus, Lemma

implies that
B(u^{\prime\prime})\subseteq B(u^{\prime})
. This implies that
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime})\leq\mathit{low}(u^{\prime\prime})
. But we have

and
\mathit{low}(u^{\prime\prime})<\mathit{nextM}(v)
, a contradiction. This shows that
u^{\prime}
is indeed the greatest vertex in
U_{4}^{4}(v)
, and therefore we have
u^{\prime}=\tilde{u}
.

Let
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
be the predecessor of
\tilde{u}
in
H(\mathit{high}_{1}(v))
. Then, since
\tilde{u}
is lower than
u
, and
u
is neither
\tilde{u}
nor
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
, we have
u>\tilde{u}^{\prime}>\tilde{u}
. Thus, since

are in

, we have that
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
is also in

(because

is a segment of

). Thus,
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
is related as ancestor and descendant with both

and
\tilde{u}
. Therefore, we have that
u
is a proper descendant of
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
, and
\tilde{u}^{\prime}
is a proper descendant of
\tilde{u}
. Then, since
\mathit{high}(u)=\mathit{high}(\tilde{u}^{\prime})=\mathit{high}(\tilde{u})
, Lemma

implies that

. Since the graph is

.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in

. Then we have that

is a descendant of
\tilde{u}
, and therefore a descendant of

. Since

, we have
\mathit{high}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
. Thus, since

is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(\tilde{u})=\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, and therefore

is a proper ancestor of

. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Since
(u,v,w)
induces a Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cut, we have

. This implies that either

, or

, or

. The case

is rejected, since

. Thus, we have that either

Thus, we conclude that either

Lemma 11.85
.

Let
(u,v,w)
be a triple of vertices such that
u
is a proper descendant of
v
,
v
is a proper descendant of
w
, and
M(w)=M(v)
. Then there is a back-edge
e
such that
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
if and only if:
(1)

\mathit{high}(u)<v
,
(2)

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, and
(3)

w
is either the greatest or the second-greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Proof.

(
\Rightarrow
)
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
. Then
B(u)\subseteq B(v)
implies that
(x,y)\in B(v)
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
, and therefore
y<v
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(u)
, this implies that
\mathit{high}(u)<v
.
(2)
is an immediate consequence of
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
\mathit{low}(u)<w
. Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(u)
such that
y=\mathit{low}(u)
. Then
x
is a descendant of
u
, and therefore a descendant of
v
, and therefore a descendant of
w
. Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that
x
is a descendant of
y
. Thus,
x
is a common descendant of
w
and
y
, and therefore
w
and
y
are related as ancestor and descendant. Then,
y=\mathit{low}(u)<w
implies that
y
is a proper ancestor of
w
. But this shows that
(x,y)\in B(w)
, in contradiction to
B(u)\cap B(w)=\emptyset
. This shows that
\mathit{low}(u)\geq w
.

Thus, it makes sense to consider the greatest proper ancestor
w^{\prime}
of
v
such that
M(w^{\prime})=M(v)
and
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
. If
w=w^{\prime}
, then we are done. Otherwise, we can also consider the second-greatest proper ancestor
w^{\prime\prime}
of
v
such that
M(w^{\prime\prime})=M(v)
and
w^{\prime\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

Let us suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that
w
is neither
w^{\prime}
nor
w^{\prime\prime}
. Thus, we have
w<w^{\prime\prime}<w^{\prime}
. Then, since
M(w)=M(w^{\prime\prime})=M(w^{\prime})
, we have that

is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime\prime}
,

is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and Lemma
6.2
implies that
B(w)\subseteq B(w^{\prime\prime})\subseteq B(w^{\prime})
. Since the graph is
3
-edge-connected, this can be strengthened to
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime\prime})\subset B(w^{\prime})
. Notice that, since
w^{\prime}\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, we have
B(u)\cap B(w^{\prime})=\emptyset
(because the lower endpoint of every back-edge in
B(u)
is not low enough to be a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
).

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in
B(w^{\prime})
. Then
x
is a descendant of
M(w^{\prime})
, and therefore a descendant of
M(v)
, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,
y
is a proper ancestor of
w^{\prime}
, and therefore
y
is a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Then
B(v)=(B(u)\sqcup B(w))\sqcup\{e\}
implies that either
(x,y)\in B(u)
, or
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. The case
(x,y)\in B(u)
is rejected, because
B(u)\cap B(w^{\prime})=\emptyset
. Thus, we have that either
(x,y)\in B(w)
, or
(x,y)=e
. Due to the generality of
(x,y)\in B(w^{\prime})
, this implies that
B(w^{\prime})\subseteq B(w)\sqcup\{e\}
. Thus, we have
B(w)\subset B(w^{\prime\prime})\subset B(w^{\prime})\subseteq B(w)\sqcup\{e\}
. But this implies that
\mathit{bcount}(w)<\mathit{bcount}(w^{\prime\prime})<\mathit{bcount}(w^{\prime})\leq\mathit{bcount}(w)+1
, which is impossible (because those number are integers).

Thus, we have that

is either the greatest or the second-greatest proper ancestor of
v
such that
M(w)=M(v)
and
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
.

(
\Leftarrow
) Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in

. Then
x
is a descendant of

, and therefore a descendant of
v
. Furthermore,

is an ancestor of
\mathit{high}(u)

, and therefore

(due to

). Since
(x,y)
is a back-edge, we have that

is a descendant of

. Thus,

is a common descendant of

and
y
, and therefore

and

. This shows that

. Due to the generality of

.

Let
(x,y)
be a back-edge in

. Then

is a descendant of

. Furthermore,

is a proper ancestor of
w
, and therefore a proper ancestor of
v
. This shows that
(x,y)\in B(v)
. Due to the generality of

, this implies that

.
Since
w\leq\mathit{low}(u)
, we infer that

(because the lower endpoint of every back-edge in

is not low enough to be a proper ancestor of

Now, since

,

\mathit{bcount}(v)=\mathit{bcount}(u)+\mathit{bcount}(w)+1

According to Proposition

, Algorithm

computes all Type-3

or

that is maximal w.r.t. the property that its elements are related as ancestor and descendant. However, in this particular case, this is not necessarily true. (See Figure

Figure 26:
In this example we have that
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
is a Type-
3\beta

4

4

Notice that, if such a
4
-cut exists, then we have that there are two distinct back-edges with the same lower endpoint: i.e., the back-edge

whose lower endpoint is

Definition 11.87

(Vertex Splitting)
.

Let
v
be a vertex of
G
, and let
(E_{1},E_{2})
be an ordered bipartition of
\partial(v)
. Let
G^{\prime}
be the graph that is formed from
G
by replacing
v
with two vertices
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
, and by inserting five multiple edges of the form
(v_{1},v_{2})
, one edge
(v_{1},z)
for every
z
such that there is an edge
(v,z)\in E_{1}
, and one edge
(v_{2},z)
for every
z
such that there is an edge
(v,z)\in E_{2}
. Then,
G^{\prime}
is called
the graph that is derived from
G
by splitting
v
at
(E_{1},E_{2})
as
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
. (See Figure
27
.)

We also define the corresponding mapping of edges
f:E(G)\rightarrow E(G^{\prime})
as follows. If
(x,y)
is an edge of
G
such that none of
x,y
is
v
, then
f((x,y))=(x,y)
. Otherwise, if, say,
x=v
, then
(x,y)
belongs to one of the sets

or
E_{2}
. If
(x,y)\in E_{1}
, then
f((x,y))=(v_{1},y)
. Otherwise,
f((x,y))=(v_{2},y)
.

A more precise definition of
f
would require that it maintains the unique identifiers of the multiple edges. For the sake of simplicity, however, we omit this consideration from the definition and from the arguments that follow.

Figure 27:
Splitting a vertex
v
at
(E_{1},E_{2})
as
v_{1}

A graph
G^{\prime}
that is derived from
G
by splitting a vertex maintains all
4
-cuts, as shown in the following.

Lemma 11.88
.

Let
G^{\prime}
be the graph that is derived from
G
by splitting a vertex
v
at
(E_{1},E_{2})
as
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
, and let
f:E(G)\rightarrow E(G^{\prime})
be the corresponding mapping of edges. Then,
G^{\prime}
is
3
-edge-connected. Furthermore, if
C
is a
4
-cut of
G
, then
f(C)
is a
4
-cut of
G^{\prime}
. Conversely, if
C^{\prime}
is a
4
-cut of
G^{\prime}
, then none of the edges in
C^{\prime}
has the form
(v_{1},v_{2})
, and
f^{-1}(C^{\prime})
is a
4
-cut of
G
.

Proof.

In order to prove this lemma, we establish a correspondence between paths in
G
and paths in
G^{\prime}
. This basically works by replacing every part of a path in
G
that passes from
v
, with a part in
G^{\prime}
that passes from
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
. More precisely, we define the correspondence as follows.

Let
P=x_{1},e_{1},x_{2},\dots,e_{k-1},x_{k}
be a path in
G
. We perform the following substitutions.

•

If
x_{1}=v
, then
e_{1}
has the form
(v,z)
, and we have that either
e_{1}\in E_{1}
or
e_{1}\in E_{2}
. If
e_{1}\in E_{1}
, then we replace the part
x_{1},e_{1}
in
P
with
v_{1},(v_{1},z)
. Otherwise, if
e_{1}\in E_{2}
, then we replace the part
x_{1},e_{1}
in
P
with
v_{2},(v_{2},z)
.

•

If
x_{k}=v
, then
e_{k-1}
has the form
(z,v)
, and we have that either
e_{k-1}\in E_{1}
or
e_{k-1}\in E_{2}
. If
e_{k-1}\in E_{1}
, then we replace the part
e_{k-1},v
in
P
with
(z,v_{1}),v_{1}
. Otherwise, if
e_{k-1}\in E_{2}
, then we replace the part
e_{k-1},v
in
P
with
(z,v_{2}),v_{2}
.

•

If there is a part
e_{i},v,e_{i+1}
in
P
, for some
i\in\{1,\dots,k-2\}
, then we have that the edge
e_{i}
has the form
(z,v)
, the edge
e_{i+1}
has the form
(v,z^{\prime})
, and there are four different cases to consider, depending on whether
e_{i}
and
e_{i+1}
are in
E_{1}
or
E_{2}
. If
e_{i}\in E_{1}
and
e_{i+1}\in E_{1}
, then we replace the part
(z,v),v,(v,z^{\prime})
with
(z,v_{1}),v_{1},(v_{1},z^{\prime})
. If
e_{i}\in E_{1}
and
e_{i+1}\in E_{2}
, then we replace the part
(z,v),v,(v,z^{\prime})
with
(z,v_{1}),v_{1},(v_{1},v_{2}),v_{2},(v_{2},z^{\prime})
. If
e_{i}\in E_{2}
and
e_{i+1}\in E_{1}
, then we replace the part
(z,v),v,(v,z^{\prime})
with
(z,v_{2}),v_{2},(v_{2},v_{1}),v_{1},(v_{1},z^{\prime})
. And if
e_{i}\in E_{2}
and
e_{i+1}\in E_{2}
, then we replace the part
(z,v),v,(v,z^{\prime})
with
(z,v_{2}),v_{2},(v_{2},z^{\prime})
.

We denote the resulting sequence as
P^{\prime}
. Observe the following facts.

1.

P^{\prime}
is a path in
G^{\prime}
.

2.

Every occurrence of a vertex
x\neq v
in
P
is maintained in
P^{\prime}
.

3.

Every occurrence of
v
in
P
, is substituted with either
v_{1}
, or
v_{2}
, or
v_{1},(v_{1},v_{2}),v_{2}
, or
v_{2},(v_{2},v_{1}),v_{1}
.

4.

Every occurrence of an edge
e
in
P
, is substituted with
f(e)
.

5.

Every part
e,v,e^{\prime}
in
P
(where
e
and
e^{\prime}
are edges), is substituted with either
f(e),v_{1},f(e^{\prime})
, or
f(e),v_{2},f(e^{\prime})
, or
f(e),v_{1},(v_{1},v_{2}),v_{2},f(e^{\prime})
, or
f(e),v_{2},(v_{2},v_{1}),v_{1},f(e^{\prime})
.

Conversely, let
Q=x_{1},e_{1},x_{2},\dots,e_{k-1},x_{k}
be a path in
G^{\prime}
. We perform the following substitutions.

•

If
x_{i}
is
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
, and
x_{i+1}
is not
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
, for some
i\in\{1,\dots,k-2\}
, then
x_{i},e_{i}
is replaced with
v,(v,x_{i+1})
.

•

If
x_{i}
is
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
, and
x_{i-1}
is not
v_{1}
or
v_{2}
, for some
i\in\{2,\dots,k-1\}
, then
e_{i-1},x_{i}
is replaced with
(x_{i-1},v),v
.

•

Every maximal segment of the form
v_{i},(v_{i},v_{j}),v_{j}
, for
i,j\in\{1,2\}
, is replaced with
v
.

We denote the resulting sequence as
\widetilde{Q}
. (Notice that after performing simultaneously the above substitutions, there may appear some segments of the form
v,v,v,\dots
. We replace those maximal segments with
v
, so that we indeed have a path. For example,

may contain the segment

, where

. Then we replace this segment with

in
\widetilde{Q}
.) Observe the following facts.

1.

\widetilde{Q}
is a path in
G
.

2.

Every occurrence of a vertex

in

is maintained in
\widetilde{Q}
.

3.

Every occurrence of

or

in

.

4.

Every occurrence of an edge

in

, is substituted with

.

Now it is easy to see why

Now the idea is to repeatedly split vertices on
T
, so that the resulting DFS-tree has the property that no two back-edges that correspond to back-edges of the original graph can have the same lower endpoint. So let
v
be a vertex, and let
(x_{1},v),\dots,(x_{k},v)
be all the incoming back-edges to
v
. We may assume that
v\neq r
(because this is sufficient for our purposes). If
k=1
, then there is nothing to do, because there is only one back-edge whose lower endpoint is
v
. Otherwise, let
(c_{1},v),\dots,(c_{t},v)
be the parent edges of the children of
v
(if it has any), and let
(v,y_{1}),\dots,(v,y_{l})
be the back-edges that stem from
v
. Then, we have
\partial(v)=\{(x_{1},v),\dots,(x_{k},v)\}\cup\{(c_{1},v),\dots,(c_{t},v)\}\cup\{(v,y_{1}),\dots,(v,y_{l})\}\cup\{(v,p(v))\}
. Let
E_{1}=\{(x_{1},v)\}\cup\{(c_{1},v),\dots,(c_{t},v)\}
, and let
E_{2}=\partial(v)\setminus{E_{1}}
. Then, we split
v
at
P=(E_{1},E_{2})
as
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
, while maintaining the DFS-tree structure (see Figure
28
). To be specific, we detach
v
from
T
, and we introduce the vertices
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
that replace
v
, such that
v_{2}=p(v_{1})
. Then,
v_{1}
inherits the children of
v
and the back-edge
(x_{1},v)
(as
(x_{1},v_{1})
), and
v_{2}
inherits the remaining edges from
\partial(v)
. Thus, we introduce the parent edges
(c_{1},v_{1}),\dots,(c_{t},v_{1})
, four back-edges of the form
(v_{1},v_{2})
(because we already have
(v_{1},v_{2})
as a parent edge), we set
p(v_{2})\leftarrow p(v)
(where
p(v)
was the parent of
v
before its deletion), and we also put back the remaining back-edges from
\partial(v)
as
(x_{2},v_{2}),\dots,(x_{k},v_{2})
and
(v_{2},y_{1}),\dots,(v_{2},y_{l})
. We refer to Figure
28
for a depiction of this process.

Figure 28:
Splitting a vertex
v
on a DFS-tree, so that the number of back-edges with lower endpoint
v
is reduced by one. With green are shown the target back-edges (incoming to

) that we want to separate w.r.t. their lower endpoint. With red is shown the back-edge that was separated from the rest and is now unique with the property of having the lower endpoint that it has. With orange are shown the five multiple edges that join the two vertices into which the vertex was split. We note that one of those multiple edges is a tree-edge, and the rest are back-edges.

In this way, we have achieved the following things. First, we have maintained a DFS-tree for the graph that is derived from
G
by splitting

at

, and second, we have effectively reduced the number of back-edges with lower endpoint

by one (i.e., now all of these, except one, have

as their lower endpoint). Now, if

, then we continue this process, by splitting
v_{2}
, until eventually we have separated the back-edges with lower endpoint

into back-edges with different lower endpoints. Then, we continue this process for all vertices
\neq r
. Let
G^{\prime}
be the resulting graph, and let

be the corresponding DFS-tree. Notice that, by Lemma
11.88
, all
4
-cuts of

that contain at least one back-edge (w.r.t.

) whose lower endpoint is not

, correspond to

-cuts of
G^{\prime}
that also have at least one back-edge (w.r.t.

). Thus, we can compute all Type-3
\beta
ii-
4

4
-cuts of
G
of the form
\{(u,p(u)),(v,p(v)),(w,p(w)),e\}
, where

is a descendant of
v
,

is a descendant of
w
,
M(B(v)\setminus\{e\})=M(v)
,
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)=\mathit{high}(u)
, and the lower endpoint of

is
\mathit{high}_{1}(v)
, by simply computing all
4

that contain three tree-edges and one back-edge, using the algorithms that we have developed so far (since our analysis covers all cases, except this one, which may only arise due to the existence of at least two back-edges with the same lower endpoint).

It remains to show how we can efficiently perform all those splittings in linear time in total. This can be done easily, because it is essentially sufficient to determine the final vertices and the edges of
G^{\prime}
, and the parent relation of the vertices of
G^{\prime}
. Then we may run a DFS with start vertex
r
, in order to assign a DFS numbering, determine the back-edges, and compute the DFS parameters that we need.

Let us describe in detail how to construct the vertices and the edges of the final graph
G^{\prime}
. First, for every vertex
v
, let
\mathit{in}(v)
denote the number of incoming back-edges to

. Then, for every vertex

such that

, we will perform

. This will substitute

with
\mathit{in}(v)

will be used in order to inherit one of the incoming back-edges to

, we create five multiple edges of the form

; one of these edges will be the parent edge of
v_{i}
. Among the
\mathit{in}(v)

v
, we let

inherit the children edges of

, and we let

inherit the outgoing back-edges from

and the parent edge
(v,p(v))
(if

). Thus, let
c
be a child of
v
. Then the parent edge of
c
is replaced with
(c_{\mathit{in}(c)},v_{1})
if
\mathit{in}(c)>1
, or with
(c,v_{1})
otherwise. Now let
e_{1},\dots,e_{\mathit{in}(v)}
be the list of the incoming back-edges to
v
. Let
i
be an index in
\{1,\dots,\mathit{in}(v)\}
, and let
e_{i}=(x,v)
. Then
e_{i}
is replaced with
(x_{\mathit{in}(x)},v_{i})
if
\mathit{in}(x)>1
, or with
(x,v_{i})
otherwise. It is not difficult to see that this construction can be completed in linear time.
